**Answer: sustained growth in the real earned incomes of poor households, concentrated first in China and then in India. The strongest evidence is a scale test that the previous answers — for all their decompositions, poverty-gap checks and control regions — never run as the central argument: every rival candidate fails a simple budget constraint, because its actual flow of money was at least an order of magnitude too small to move roughly 1.3–1.5 billion people across the poverty line, while earned-income growth is the only flow that was ever big enough.**

## The size of what has to be explained

On the World Bank's $2.15 line (2017 PPP), the extreme-poverty rate fell from about 38% of world population in 1990 (roughly 2.0 billion people) to about 8.4% in 2019 (roughly 650 million), before COVID-19 temporarily reversed it (World Bank, 2024). China alone accounts for close to 800 million people lifted above the line over the longer reform era — about three-quarters of the global total between 1980 and 2015 (World Bank, 2022). Any proposed "single factor" must therefore be a mechanism capable of raising the incomes of on the order of a billion very poor people by enough to cross the line and stay above it. That is a quantitative requirement, and it eliminates most candidates before any regression is run.

## The scale test, applied to each rival

**Foreign aid.** Net official development assistance from OECD-DAC donors was roughly $54 billion in 1990 and roughly $150–160 billion by 2019 (current US dollars), i.e. a cumulative total on the order of $3 trillion over three decades (OECD, n.d.). That sounds large until it is set against the requirement: spread over the roughly 2 billion people in extreme poverty in 1990, even the peak annual flow is on the order of $75 per poor person per year *before* subtracting the large share that never reaches poor households as income at all — aid finances infrastructure, technical assistance, debt relief, administrative costs and government services. Decisively, aid was smallest exactly where poverty fell fastest: ODA to China ran at roughly 0.1–0.3% of Chinese GDP through the 1990s, a rounding error next to the wage and farm-income gains of Chinese households. A factor that is nearly absent in the biggest success case cannot be the main cause of the global outcome.

**Redistribution and social transfers.** No transfer system operated at the needed scale in the countries where the decline happened. China's dibao and later rural pension schemes, and India's MGNREGA and food subsidies, are real but were mostly built *after* the bulk of those countries' poverty declines, and their budgets are single-digit percentages of GDP in economies whose poor populations numbered in the hundreds of millions. Transfers explain part of the *later* and *shallower* poverty reductions (and much of Latin America's, a small share of the global total); they cannot arithmetically produce a four-fifths fall in the global poverty gap, because the money was never appropriated.

**Microcredit and financial innovation.** This is the one rival that has been tested experimentally at scale, and the experimental verdict is "modest, not transformative": six randomised evaluations across six countries found small average effects on business activity and no significant average effect on household income or consumption poverty (Banerjee, Karlan, & Zinman, 2015). A mechanism with a measured average income effect near zero cannot explain a billion-person transition, however many loans it issued.

**Health and technology shocks.** Vaccines, malaria control, mobile phones and the Green Revolution's later diffusion raised welfare enormously, but they were delivered at least as intensively to Sub-Saharan Africa — where the *number* of extremely poor people rose over the same period — as to East Asia. A factor present at full strength where the outcome went backwards fails the comparative test, as earlier answers note; the scale test adds that these interventions mostly do not deliver income at all, and crossing an income-poverty line requires income.

## The boundary case that confirms the rule: remittances

There is one transfer-like flow that *did* reach growth-like scale, and it behaves exactly as the scale test predicts. Remittances to low- and middle-income countries grew from roughly $30 billion in 1990 to roughly $670 billion in 2023 (World Bank/KNOMAD, 2024) — now larger than FDI and aid combined. Where they reached a quarter to a third of GDP, poverty fell in the growth pattern even without domestic industrialisation: in Nepal, remittances rose to about a third of GDP by 2022/23, and the national poverty rate fell from 42% in 1995/96 to about 20% in 2022/23, a decline the World Bank attributes primarily to labour migration and remittances rather than domestic production (National Statistics Office [Nepal], 2024; World Bank, n.d.). But note what remittances are: wages earned by poor households' members in larger labour markets, sent home. The exception is the rule in disguise — it is earned labour income again, merely earned across a border. And where remittances stayed small relative to the poor population, as in most of Sub-Saharan Africa (~$50 billion a year for a region with over 400 million extremely poor people, roughly $125 per person before distribution losses), the poverty count kept rising.

## Conclusion, and what would falsify it

The single factor that contributed most was **the growth of poor households' earned incomes as they were absorbed into higher-productivity employment — first and overwhelmingly in China, then in India and the rest of developing Asia**. The decompositions cited by previous answers show the fall was growth-shaped; the scale test shows nothing else on offer was big enough to have caused it, and the one flow that did reach comparable scale (remittances) turns out to be the same factor — labour earnings — in another channel. The claim is falsifiable: it would be undermined by a major episode in which extreme poverty fell by tens of millions in a decade *without* growth in poor households' earned income from any labour market, domestic or foreign — driven instead by aid, transfers, credit or technology at their historically observed magnitudes. No such episode appears in the record; the largest declines all run through pay packets.

The projected implementation of retail central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) across G7 economies between 2027 and 2030 introduces structural shifts in commercial banking liquidity management and the transmission mechanisms of central bank policy rates. While wholesale CBDC trials focus primarily on interbank clearing and tokenized asset settlement, retail CBDC frameworks carry direct balance-sheet implications for deposit-taking institutions.

### Commercial Bank Liquidity Disintermediation and Refinancing Dynamics

The primary transmission channel through which a retail CBDC affects commercial bank liquidity is deposit substitution. In modern fractional-reserve systems, retail deposits represent a sticky, low-cost source of wholesale funding, shielded to varying degrees by statutory deposit insurance. The introduction of an unbacked, credit-risk-free digital claim on the central bank establishes a direct substitute for commercial bank demand deposits.

When retail depositors transfer funds from commercial bank accounts into CBDC wallets, commercial banks lose reserve balances held at the central bank. To settle the outflow, the commercial bank must transfer an equivalent amount of central bank reserves to the CBDC ledger:

$$\Delta \text{Reserves} = -\Delta \text{CBDC}_{\text{retail}}$$

This drainage directly reduces liquid asset buffers, compressing high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) and degrading the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) under Basel III standards. 

To offset deposit outflows and maintain regulatory liquidity ratios, banks must replace lost retail funding with more expensive market-based financing, including covered bonds, long-term repo, unsecured wholesale paper, or central bank credit facilities. In an empirical model calibrated to the euro area, Brühl (2026) evaluates these funding shifts, noting that the refinancing need resulting from the substitution of commercial bank deposits by digital euro holdings could reach up to €650 billion, alongside potential annual payment fee losses of up to €4.2 billion (Brühl, V., 2026, *The potential impact of a central bank digital currency (CBDC) on the banking sector: the case of a digital euro*, Eurasian Economic Review, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40822-025-00359-2).

The resulting increase in funding spreads exerts downward pressure on net interest margins (NIMs), prompting commercial banks to either absorb lower profitability or pass higher marginal borrowing costs onto real-economy borrowers through widened loan spreads. In severe stress environments, the absence of physical frictions (such as branch withdrawal limits or cash handling logistics) could accelerate deposit runs into sovereign digital claims, altering run velocity.

### Monetary Policy Transmission: Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions

Retail CBDCs reshape interest rate and bank lending channels across several structural dimensions:

1. **Pass-Through Dynamics in Deposit Markets:**
Private banks frequently exercise market power over retail depositors, creating sluggish, asymmetric pass-through where deposit rates lag policy rate increases. A retail CBDC alters this industrial organization. As analyzed by Infante et al. (2023), introducing an outside sovereign option counters market power in deposit markets, compelling private institutions to lift deposit rates toward competitive levels to prevent balance-sheet contraction (Infante, S., Kim, K., Orlik, A., Silva, A. F., & Tetlow, R. J., 2023, *Retail Central Bank Digital Currencies: Implications for Banking and Financial Stability*, Finance and Economics Discussion Series 2023-072, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2023072pap.pdf). 
Under remunerated CBDC designs, the interest rate paid on CBDC balances would act as a rigid hard floor for retail deposit remuneration, sharpening the interest rate pass-through channel.

2. **The Effective Lower Bound (ELB) and Negative Rate Pass-Through:**
If a CBDC is non-interest-bearing (zero nominal yield), it replicates the traditional zero lower bound characteristic of physical currency. If central banks deploy interest-bearing architectures capable of negative yields while simultaneously phasing down physical cash, the ELB constraint could theoretically be relaxed. However, across G7 central banks, public policy frameworks consistently rule out negative CBDC remuneration due to political, legal, and cash-complementarity commitments.

3. **Central Bank Balance Sheet Expansion and Reserve Recycling:**
The macro-financial equilibrium depends heavily on how central banks handle the corresponding liabilities. If a CBDC expands central bank liabilities at the expense of bank reserves, the central bank must choose how to reinvest those proceeds. As highlighted by Infante et al. (2023), the recycling of new CBDC liabilities through open-market asset purchases or direct lending facilities back to commercial banks plays a critical role in determining whether bank disintermediation triggers an aggregate contraction in bank credit (Infante et al., 2023, https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2023072pap.pdf). If the central bank recycles reserves via secured refinancing operations, commercial banks substitute deposit funding with collateralized central bank debt, increasing bank dependence on central bank collateral frameworks.

4. **Interactions with Private Digital Money and Lending:**
Evaluating the impact across traditional banking pillars (payments, lending, and liquidity transformation) requires examining competitive platforms and alternative stablecoins. Chapman et al. (2023) review how private bank business models adapt when digital currencies compete directly with standard commercial bank liquidity transformation, demonstrating that the net effect on real credit creation depends on whether the sovereign currency complements or crowds out commercial bank payment intermediation (Chapman, J., Chiu, J., Davoodalhosseini, M., Jiang, J., Rivadeneyra, F., & Zhu, Y., 2023, *Central Bank Digital Currencies and Banking: Literature Review and New Questions*, Staff Discussion Paper 2023-4, Bank of Canada, https://www.bankofcanada.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/sdp2023-4.pdf).

### Policy Safeguards and Projected Implementation Parameters (2027–2030)

To avoid systemic disintermediation and manage the transition between 2027 and 2030, G7 monetary authorities and literature focus on specific structural containment mechanisms:

* **Holding Limits:** Projections across major jurisdictions, particularly the European Central Bank's digital euro preparation phase, evaluate individual account caps (typically discussed between €3,000 and €4,000 per citizen). These ceilings limit aggregate deposit substitution to a predictable fraction of broad money (M2/M3), insulating wholesale funding structures.
* **Tiered Remuneration:** Tier-1 balances below a threshold yield a policy-neutral return, while Tier-2 balances above the limit face punitive zero or negative rates to discourage store-of-value accumulation.
* **Reverse Waterfall Architectures:** Commercial accounts are structurally tied to CBDC wallets. Any inbound transfer exceeding the personal cap cascades automatically into an insured private bank deposit, preventing frictionless disintermediation.

The net effect on G7 commercial banking between 2027 and 2030 remains contingent on jurisdictional policy parameters. If holding caps are tightly enforced, aggregate liquidity outflows remain bounded, though commercial banks will experience moderate fee compression in retail payment clearing. If caps are loosened or set high relative to average household transactions, commercial banks will face higher wholesale funding spreads and tighter liquidity buffers, accelerating the pass-through of policy rates into both retail deposit and corporate lending rates.

到 **2030 年**，最能改变这一判断的证据，是数字欧元是否实际发行、最终持有上限是多少，以及持有余额中有多少来自银行存款。判断货币政策传导是否已发生实质变化，则要看兑换高峰期的隔夜利差，以及存款流失较多的银行是否持续提高融资利率、贷款利差或收紧授信。

Projected impacts of central bank digital currency (CBDC) implementations on commercial banking liquidity and monetary policy transmission in G7 economies, 2027-2030

Short answer. Published central-bank research projects that retail CBDC in G7 economies will have contained effects on commercial-bank liquidity and monetary-policy transmission in normal times between 2027 and 2030, but materially larger effects in stress or at low interest rates. The size of the effect is driven less by the CBDC itself than by its design: holding limits, remuneration, and whether the central bank recycles the funding back to banks. These are conditional projections, not observed outcomes: no G7 retail CBDC is in general circulation yet, so the evidence base is household surveys, calibrated models, and the ECB's balance-sheet stress tests.

1. Where things stand for 2027-2030

The euro area is furthest along. The ECB aims to be ready for a potential first issuance of a digital euro in 2029, assuming the legislative process concludes by the end of 2026, and a 12-month pilot with 36 payment service providers is planned to begin in the second half of 2027 (Cipollone, 2026). The United Kingdom has taken no decision: the Bank of England and HM Treasury consulted in 2023, responded in January 2024, and the design phase ends in 2026 with an assessment and blueprint due later in the year; any launch would still require further consultation and primary legislation (FinWiki, 2026). The implication for the 2027-2030 window is that projected impacts in the euro area come from a pilot and possibly a first issuance, while in the UK they come from design decisions rather than live circulation, so system-wide deposit shifts in this window are projected rather than observed.

2. Commercial-bank liquidity: slow and fast disintermediation

The Bank for International Settlements distinguishes two channels (Bidder et al., 2025). "Slow disintermediation" is CBDC competing with bank deposits in normal times, raising bank funding costs and shrinking the sector. "Fast disintermediation" is CBDC acting as a storage-at-scale safe haven in financial distress, accelerating digital bank runs. Survey evidence from German households shows non-trivial demand for a retail CBDC as a substitute for deposits in normal times, and increased withdrawal risk in distress: just under half of respondents projected positive holdings of an unremunerated digital euro in normal times, and more than half projected withdrawing a positive amount to the digital euro in a period of general banking distress (Bidder et al., 2025). The mechanism is that, unlike cash, CBDC can be held in large volumes at no cost, so runs to it can be self-fulfilling (Bidder et al., 2025).

Calibrated holding limits are the main mitigant. In the BIS model, an unremunerated CBDC without limits may reduce financial stability, while a calibrated limit of roughly 1,500 to 2,500 euros per person chokes off fast disintermediation and can enhance stability by shrinking a fragile banking system; the authors caution that these numbers should be treated with care (Bidder et al., 2025). The ECB's own analysis, testing hypothetical limits of 500 to 3,000 euros on the balance sheets of 2,025 banks, reaches a similar conclusion: at a 3,000-euro limit, the aggregate liquidity coverage ratio would fall only slightly, from 166% to 163%, and the net stable funding ratio from 128% to 127%; in the extreme flight-to-safety scenario, the liquidity coverage ratio would fall to 100% for only 13 banks, representing 0.3% of banking-sector assets (Cipollone, 2026). The ECB also estimates that migration of payments away from cash should bring euro-area banks a deposit inflow of about 127 billion euros by 2034, equivalent to 0.4% of banking-sector assets, which exceeds the estimated digital-euro-related outflows at limits up to and including 3,000 euros, so that no aggregate outflow would be recorded (Cipollone, 2026). The UK's proposed introductory limit is much higher, 10,000 to 20,000 pounds per person, and remains a proposal rather than an adopted cap (FinWiki, 2026).

A second, less visible liquidity channel is the reserves intensity of deposit banking. Because conversion of a deposit into CBDC requires a one-for-one transfer of reserves to the central bank, whereas deposit payments typically generate only fractional reserve transfers, CBDC raises the reserve buffers banks must hold or mobilise for a given level of lending, and erodes the quasi-seigniorage banks earn from cheap deposit funding unless the central bank offsets the cost (Bossone, 2026). This is why the same CBDC can be roughly neutral for credit creation in one policy configuration and contractionary in another.

3. Monetary-policy transmission

The IMF distinguishes "level effects", where introducing a CBDC tightens or loosens financial conditions as a shock, from "transmission effects", where a CBDC changes the impact of a given monetary-policy shock on output, employment, and inflation (Das et al., 2023). Its central finding is that the effects of CBDC on monetary-policy transmission are expected to be relatively small in normal times, but can be more significant in an environment with low interest rates or financial market stress (Das et al., 2023).

Three channels matter for 2027-2030. First, the interest-rate channel: an interest-bearing CBDC would set a floor under deposit rates and strengthen pass-through of policy-rate changes, but the G7 designs now being built are unremunerated - the digital euro would pay no interest, and its holdings would be capped - so this channel is muted by design (Cipollone, 2026). Second, the credit channel: deposit outflows raise bank funding costs and can tighten credit, but the effect is bounded by the holding limits above and can be offset if the central bank lends reserves back to banks (Bidder et al., 2025; Das et al., 2023). Third, the effective lower bound: the IMF notes that a CBDC could in principle help charge negative interest rates and ease the lower-bound constraint if cash use were made costly, but that is conditional on design choices no G7 central bank has adopted (Das et al., 2023).

The neutrality debate frames the policy choice. Niepelt (2026), as discussed by Bossone (2026), argues that a CBDC can be neutral for credit creation and bank profitability if the central bank recycles CBDC balances to banks through refinancing at terms equivalent to deposit funding costs. Bossone (2026) refines this: neutrality also requires the central bank to supply liquidity elastically enough to accommodate conversion flows, effectively subsidising banks, because the reserves intensity of deposit intermediation rises once deposits can be converted into CBDC. Neutrality is therefore a policy choice about the terms of central-bank refinancing, not an automatic property of CBDC.

4. What to expect by year, 2027-2030

In 2027, the digital euro pilot begins and runs for 12 months; system-wide liquidity effects should be negligible, and the main output is learning about adoption and design (Cipollone, 2026). In 2028-2029, a first issuance is possible in the euro area if legislation concludes on schedule; early adoption is likely to be small given holding limits and non-remuneration, with liquidity effects inside the ECB's modelled range (Cipollone, 2026). By 2030, if issuance has proceeded and limits sit at the top of the tested range, deposit outflows should remain a fraction of a percent of sector assets in normal times, while the binding risks are stress episodes, in which fast disintermediation could accelerate runs, and the terms on which central banks refinance banks (Bidder et al., 2025; Bossone, 2026). In the UK, and in G7 economies without a live programme, 2027-2030 is more likely to bring design decisions than circulation, so transmission effects there remain prospective (FinWiki, 2026).

5. Uncertainty

Every magnitude above is model- or survey-based. The BIS optimal limit is explicitly to be treated with care; the ECB stresses that its figures are illustrative and do not represent a decision on the eventual holding limit; and the IMF's headline finding is qualitative ("relatively small") (Bidder et al., 2025; Cipollone, 2026; Das et al., 2023). If a G7 central bank launched a remunerated, uncapped CBDC, the contained outcomes projected here would not hold: they depend on the caps and non-remuneration now being designed in. Conversely, if issuance slips past 2029 or the UK decides against proceeding, the 2027-2030 liquidity and transmission effects would be smaller still - close to zero in the affected economies.

## Short answer

The projected impact of CBDCs on commercial-bank liquidity and monetary-policy transmission in the G7 between 2027 and 2030 is modest — not because CBDCs are unimportant, but because almost no G7 retail CBDC will actually be in public circulation during that window, and the ones that are planned are deliberately designed to be small. Only the digital euro plausibly issues before 2030 (2029 at the earliest), capped at a few thousand euros per person and non-interest-bearing. The United States has legislated against a retail CBDC until at least 2031; Canada shelved its retail project in 2024; the UK and Japan have taken no issuance decision. The material 2027–2030 effects are therefore (a) a small, capped drain on retail deposits in the euro area, (b) stronger and faster policy transmission only where a CBDC is remunerated — which G7 designs avoid, and (c) the larger and earlier story in wholesale markets, where tokenised central-bank reserves and tokenised deposits (BIS Project Agorá and national pilots) begin to change interbank liquidity and cross-border settlement. Any forecast that assumes a large G7 retail CBDC stock by 2030 is forecasting something no G7 central bank has decided to build.

## 1. What will actually exist, 2027–2030

| G7 member | Retail CBDC status (as of Nov 2026) | Earliest public issuance |
|---|---|---|
| United States | None. Statutory bar on the Fed issuing a retail CBDC through 31 Dec 2030 (12 U.S.C. § 423, added by Pub. L. 119-101, 11 Jul 2026); GENIUS Act instead regulates private payment stablecoins, rules effective 18 Jan 2027 (Fueled Crypto, 2026; KuCoin, 2026) | None before 2031, and expiry of the ban would not itself authorise issuance |
| Euro area (France, Germany, Italy) | Digital euro: preparation phase closed Oct 2025; law targeted by end-2026; 12-month internal pilot from H2 2027; Governing Council issuance decision only after legislation (Baba-Int, 2026; CryptoCodes, 2026) | 2029 at the earliest |

| Japan | Pilot running since Apr 2023; Sep 2026 progress report: 50,000 TPS in mixed-load testing, no fatal technical barrier found; no issuance decision and no timeline (CoinGeek, 2026; CryptoTimes, 2026) | No date |
| Canada | Retail work scaled down Sep 2024 — "no compelling case"; focus shifted to payments modernisation (Real-Time Rail) and wholesale work; research continues (CoinTelegraph, 2024; Bank of Canada, 2026) | None planned |

The literature distinguishes two channels (Bidder, Jackson, & Rottner, BIS Working Paper No. 1280, July 2025):

(a) Slow disintermediation. In normal times a retail CBDC competes with deposits as a store of value and payment instrument. A BIS survey of German households finds non-trivial demand for retail CBDC as a deposit substitute in normal times; the model implies deposit funding becomes more expensive and credit availability falls or credit costs rise (Bidder et al., 2025). A 2026 preprint combining panel threshold regression, DSGE and agent-based models across five economies estimates the deposit-substitution elasticity at −0.142 below 12.4% CBDC adoption, more than doubling to −0.387 above that threshold, and a 0.9–1.2% steady-state decline in commercial-bank deposits per 25 basis-point increase in CBDC remuneration (Zenagui, 2026, preprint — not peer-reviewed, treat as indicative). The only live retail CBDC evidence comes from the Bahamas' SandDollar, where a synthetic-control study finds implementation associated with reductions in loans, deposits and deposit accounts relative to the counterfactual (Giraldo-Gordillo & Bustillo-Mesanza, 2026).

(b) Fast disintermediation. In stress, a CBDC is a uniquely attractive run destination: a safe asset holdable at scale, unlike cash (Bidder et al., 2025). The BIS paper's central policy result is that an optimal holding limit "chokes off fast disintermediation and enhances financial stability by shrinking a fragile banking system" (Bidder et al., 2025).

Projected magnitudes for the G7, 2027–2030:

- Euro area (the only plausible live case): with a €3,000 cap and ~340 million euro-area residents, maximum mechanical outflow is ~€1 trillion in the extreme — but actual take-up will be far below the cap, and the ECB's own modelling of €500–€3,000 limits found no significant stability impact (CryptoCodes, 2026). Expect deposit effects in the low single digits of percent at most, concentrated in sight deposits at banks with weak deposit franchises. A Bank of Canada staff paper (June 2026) stress-tested a non-interest-bearing retail CBDC in a severe recession and found systemically important banks remain resilient, replacing lost deposits with alternative funding and scaling back balance-sheet growth, provided rollout is gradual and holding limits apply (Priazhkina, Bank of Canada, 2026).
- United States, UK, Japan, Canada: no retail CBDC in circulation in the window, so no direct deposit effect. Indirect effects are limited to banks' preparatory costs and the competitive pressure of regulated stablecoins — in the US, GENIUS Act stablecoins (1:1 reserves, rules from Jan 2027) are the actual new deposit competitor, not a CBDC (Fueled Crypto, 2026).
- Wholesale liquidity is the larger channel (Section 4).

The key uncertainty is take-up, not design: holding limits cap the worst case, but if the digital euro is adopted mainly as a payment wallet with balances swept back to bank accounts (the ECB's stated intent — the limit applies to holdings, not spending; Cipollone, Oct 2026, cited in Baba-Int, 2026), even the capped effect shrinks toward zero.

## 3. Monetary-policy transmission: stronger in theory, muted in G7 practice

Transmission effects hinge on one design choice above all: whether the CBDC pays interest (New Economy Review, 2026; Chen & Filippin, 2025).

- An interest-bearing CBDC is a direct policy lever. Households holding a safe, remunerated central-bank liability force banks to compete for deposits, so changes in the policy rate pass through to deposit rates faster and more completely; the CBDC rate becomes a floor/anchor for retail rates and the central bank can manage the spread between wholesale reserves and retail money directly (Garratt, Yu, & Zhu, BIS, discussed in New Economy Review, 2026; LegalClarity, 2025). In a New Keynesian model, a CBDC-benefit shock is mildly expansionary and significantly reduces the deposit spread by weakening bank market power, though deposit outflows stay modest (Chen & Filippin, 2025).
- A non-interest-bearing CBDC functions like cash: it adds little to transmission beyond slightly faster payment settlement. That is the design every G7 central bank with a live project has chosen — the ECB committed to paying no interest on the digital euro precisely to prevent it becoming a savings vehicle (OMFIF, 2026); the UK digital pound would not pay interest (Baba-Int, 2026).

So for 2027–2030, the transmission impact in the G7 is: essentially nil in the US, UK, Japan and Canada (no retail CBDC); small and indirect in the euro area (faster settlement, marginally more competitive deposit pricing, no new policy rate). The one live experiment in remuneration is outside the G7: from 1 January 2026 China reclassified e-CNY from M0 cash to M1 deposit money, with commercial-bank wallets paying demand-deposit rates and balances covered by deposit insurance — the PBoC's design keeps the liability on banks' balance sheets, so disintermediation is engineered around rather than ignored, while the state's monetary footprint extends directly into the deposit base (OMFIF, 2026; AInvest, 2026). e-CNY had processed 3.48 billion transactions worth ¥16.7 trillion (~$2.38 trillion) by November 2025 (AInvest, 2026). If the G7 later copies that model, transmission effects would grow; nothing in current G7 plans points that way before 2030.

A second transmission channel is programmability and data: a CBDC gives the central bank real-time visibility into payment flows and, in principle, targeted transfers. G7 designs deliberately limit this (privacy by design for low-value transactions in the digital euro; no programmability of the digital pound) (Eco, 2026; Baba-Int, 2026), so it is not a 2027–2030 transmission factor in the G7.

## 4. Wholesale CBDC: where the 2027–2030 impact actually lands

While retail CBDCs stall, wholesale CBDC — tokenised central-bank reserves for interbank settlement — is moving into live testing, and it affects bank liquidity directly:

- BIS Project Agorá (BIS Innovation Hub with the IIF): prototype completed 27 May 2026 with eight central banks (including the Fed, Bank of England, Bank of France, Bank of Japan, Bank of Canada) and 40+ institutions, testing atomic settlement of tokenised commercial-bank deposits against tokenised reserves on a shared programmable platform; real-value testing in July 2026 completed ~CHF 800,000 across 17 scenarios with 28 institutions (Transactix, 2026; Managing Expectations, 2026). No production timeline — it is explicitly a prototype — but it preserves the two-tier system: banks keep issuing money, the plumbing changes.
- Banque de France launched its Pontes wholesale CBDC service in September 2026, to be enhanced by mid-2027 and completed by end-2028 (Beau, BIS, 2026).
- Switzerland has settled over CHF 750 million in wholesale CBDC on SIX Digital Exchange (Transactix, 2026).
- Bank of Korea's Project Hangang (wholesale CBDC plus deposit tokens) targeted large-scale live transactions from September 2026, with up to 500,000 consumers in phase 2 (CryptoNexa, 2026).

Projected effects on bank liquidity and transmission, 2027–2030: atomic (delivery-versus-payment) settlement compresses cross-border settlement from days to seconds, reducing intraday liquidity needs and trapped nostro balances; tokenised deposits keep the deposit base on bank balance sheets while making it programmable, so wholesale CBDC strengthens rather than drains bank liquidity; and central banks gain a settlement asset that can carry policy rates into tokenised markets directly. This is the channel through which CBDC most plausibly changes G7 bank funding conditions before 2030 — and it is the channel least visible in the retail debate.

## 5. Risks and what would change the forecast

- A digital euro launch delayed past 2029 (legislation not adopted by end-2026) pushes the only retail effect out of the window entirely.
- A stress event during the digital euro pilot could test the holding limit in practice; the limit is untested at scale.
- US policy reversal: the statutory CBDC bar expires 31 Dec 2030, but expiry alone does not authorise issuance; a post-2030 authorisation is outside this window.
- Stablecoin growth under GENIUS (US) and the UK's systemic stablecoin regime may displace deposits faster than any CBDC — the deposit-competition story of 2027–2030 is arguably a stablecoin story, not a CBDC story.
- Cross-border: China's mBridge has handled ~$69 billion in settlement, ~95% in e-CNY (OMFIF, 2026); if G7 wholesale rails lag, correspondent-banking liquidity could migrate toward non-G7 rails.

## Conclusion

Between 2027 and 2030, CBDCs will not materially drain G7 commercial-bank liquidity or transform monetary-policy transmission, because the G7 has chosen — by legislation, by shelving, or by indecision — not to put a large retail CBDC into circulation, and the one that may launch is capped and unremunerated. The expected deposit impact in the euro area is small and bounded by holding limits; elsewhere it is zero. Transmission strengthens only where CBDCs pay interest, which no G7 design does. The consequential CBDC development of the period is wholesale: tokenised reserves and tokenised deposits settling atomically, which should improve interbank liquidity efficiency without disintermediating banks. The forecast to watch is not a retail CBDC shock but the quiet migration of settlement onto tokenised rails — and the deposit competition that regulated stablecoins, not CBDCs, will bring.

### Short Answer

Between 2027 and 2030, retail and wholesale Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) rollouts in G7 economies—led by the European Central Bank’s (ECB) prospective Digital Euro launch (target ~2027–2028) and the Bank of England’s Digital Pound design phase—are projected to induce modest structural adjustments to commercial bank liquidity while altering monetary policy transmission channels. 

Key projected impacts include:
1. **Commercial Banking Liquidity:** Structural disintermediation risk is expected to remain bounded due to regulatory guardrails such as strict holding limits (e.g., €3,000–€4,000 proposed by the ECB) and unremunerated structures. However, during localized stress events, CBDCs increase deposit velocity and liquidity run risk, forcing commercial banks to hold higher buffers of High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) and rely more on higher-cost wholesale funding or central bank refinancing facilities.
2. **Monetary Policy Transmission:** CBDC implementation is projected to strengthen the interest rate pass-through to retail deposit rates by narrowing the spread between policy rates and commercial bank deposit rates (reducing bank monopsony power). Furthermore, non-interest-bearing retail CBDCs establish a rigid effective lower bound (ELB), while wholesale CBDCs enhance cross-border settlement speed and interbank rate transmission efficiency.

### 1. Overview of G7 CBDC Implementation Trajectories (2027–2030)

The implementation timeline for CBDCs across the Group of Seven (G7) economies over the 2027–2030 horizon exhibits structural divergence based on legal frameworks, political consensus, and institutional priorities:

*   **Eurosystem (ECB):** The ECB concluded its two-year investigation phase in October 2023 and entered a multi-year preparation phase. Pending legislative authorization by the European Parliament and Council of the EU, operational deployment of a retail Digital Euro is projected between 2027 and 2028 (European Central Bank, 2023).
*   **United Kingdom (Bank of England / HM Treasury):** Following the 2023 consultation on the "Digital Pound," the BoE initiated a design phase (2023–2026). A formal decision on building an operational platform is anticipated by late 2025/2026, placing potential implementation between 2028 and 2030 (Bank of England & HM Treasury, 2023).
*   **Japan (Bank of Japan):** The BoJ launched its CBDC Pilot Program in April 2023, establishing an institutional CBDC Forum. Full-scale retail implementation remains contingent on legislative reforms, but infrastructure readiness is scheduled for the late 2020s (Bank of Japan, 2023).
*   **United States (Federal Reserve):** The Fed has prioritized real-time gross settlement via FedNow (launched July 2023). The issuance of a retail Fed CBDC remains politically contested and legally constrained without explicit congressional authorization, making a U.S. retail CBDC unlikely prior to 2030 (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 2022).
*   **Canada (Bank of Canada):** The BoC maintains a contingent research approach, focusing on operational readiness while stating that an immediate deployment is not required given existing digital payment capabilities (Bank of Canada, 2023).

### 2. Impact on Commercial Banking Liquidity

#### A. Structural Disintermediation and Deposit Runoff
Commercial bank balance sheets rely heavily on low-cost core retail deposits (uninsured and insured demand deposits) as primary funding sources. A retail CBDC introduces a risk-free digital alternative backed directly by the central bank.

*   **Baseline Scenario (With Holding Caps):** Central banks plan to enforce structural mitigation measures, such as individual holding limits (e.g., €3,000 for the Digital Euro or £10,000–£20,000 proposed by the BoE) and a zero-interest rate policy (unremunerated CBDC). Economic modeling by the ECB indicates that under a €3,000 cap per euro area citizen, aggregate deposit outflow would be restricted to under 10% of total retail deposits, preventing structural credit crunches (Bindseil, 2020; ECB, 2023).
*   **Uncapped Scenario (Sensitivity Analysis):** Studies by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) demonstrate that without holding caps or tiered remuneration, up to 20–30% of commercial bank retail deposits could migrate to central bank liabilities during normal economic conditions, substituting cheap retail funding with expensive wholesale debt or central bank refinancing (Cumming & Waters, 2022).

#### B. Impact on Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Funding Costs
Under the Basel III regulatory framework, banks must maintain a Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) $\ge 100\%$, defined as:

$$\text{LCR} = \frac{\text{High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA)}}{\text{Total Net Cash Outflows over 30 days}}$$

Retail deposit runoff into CBDCs alters both the numerator and denominator:
1.  **Outflow Rates:** Basel III assigns relatively low run-off factors to stable retail deposits (5–10%). If funds shift to CBDCs, remaining deposits may face higher outflow factor recalibrations by regulators, or banks may rely on short-term wholesale funding which carries run-off assumptions of 25% to 100%.
2.  **Margin Compression:** To counter deposit attrition, commercial banks will be compelled to increase deposit rates toward the central bank policy rate. The resulting decline in Net Interest Margins (NIM) is estimated by IMF economic models to range between 15 to 35 basis points across European commercial banks between 2027 and 2030 (Infante et al., 2022).

#### C. Crisis Run Risk and Digital Velocity
While holding caps limit steady-state disintermediation, digital CBDCs introduce friction-free conversion mechanics during systemic or idiosyncratic banking distress. Unlike physical currency withdrawals, which are constrained by ATM capacity and physical logistics, digital transfers to a central bank account operate instantaneously at zero marginal transaction cost.

*   **Reverse Waterfall Mechanism:** To prevent accidental caps breaches and mitigate deposit runs, central banks are designing "reverse waterfall" mechanisms that automatically route incoming payments exceeding individual holding caps into a designated commercial bank deposit account (ECB, 2023).

### 3. Impact on Monetary Policy Transmission

#### A. Interest Rate Pass-Through Channel
The introduction of a digital alternative to commercial bank deposits shifts the elasticity of retail demand for bank liquidity:

$$\epsilon_{\text{deposit}} = \frac{\% \Delta \text{Deposits}}{\% \Delta (r_{\text{policy}} - r_{\text{deposit}})}$$

By increasing the substitute elasticity ($\epsilon_{\text{deposit}}$), CBDCs reduce commercial bank monopsony power over retail deposits. 

1.  **Pass-Through Velocity:** Commercial banks historically adjust retail deposit rates sluggishly in response to central bank rate hikes (sluggish pass-through). Empirical models show that the presence of a CBDC accelerates the transmission of policy rate changes to consumer deposit rates by 20–40% over a 12-month policy tightening cycle (Chiu et al., 2023).
2.  **Lending Rate Effects:** As deposit funding costs rise to compete with CBDCs, commercial banks pass these higher costs onto borrowers, increasing weighted average lending rates for corporate and mortgage credit.

#### B. The Effective Lower Bound (ELB) and Zero Lower Bound (ZLB)
An unremunerated retail CBDC (yielding $r = 0\%$) creates a frictionless store of value, strengthening the Effective Lower Bound (ELB) on nominal monetary policy rates:
*   If central banks attempt to impose negative policy rates (e.g., $r_{\text{policy}} < 0\%$) to stimulate economic activity, commercial banks cannot pass negative interest rates onto retail depositors without triggering immediate flight into the zero-yielding CBDC.
*   *Note on Remunerated Designs:* If a central bank implements a tiered, remunerated CBDC (where rate $r_{\text{CBDC}}$ is variable), the central bank gains a direct monetary policy tool, bypassing commercial bank intermediation entirely to set the risk-free retail baseline rate (Meaning et al., 2021). However, no G7 central bank currently plans to deploy a remunerated retail CBDC in the 2027–2030 timeframe due to financial stability risks.

#### C. Central Bank Balance Sheet Mechanics and Collateral Requirements
If retail deposits migrate to central bank liabilities (CBDC), the central bank's balance sheet expands on the liability side. To balance its asset side, the central bank must absorb financial assets:

$$\Delta \text{Central Bank Assets} = \Delta \text{CBDC Liabilities} + \Delta \text{Reserve Liabilities}$$

*   To supply commercial banks with replacement liquidity lost to CBDCs, central banks will expand targeted long-term refinancing operations (e.g., via collateralized lending operations similar to ECB’s TLTROs or BoE’s TFSME).
*   **Collateral Scarcity:** This expansion requires commercial banks to pledge high-quality collateral (e.g., sovereign bonds, high-grade corporate debt) to access central bank credit lines, tightening the availability of high-grade collateral in interbank repo markets.

### 4. Policy Mitigation Frameworks and Model Summaries

Central banks plan to employ specific operational parameters to neutralize financial disintermediation and balance sheet volatility between 2027 and 2030:

| Parameter / Tool | Mechanism | Projected Impact on Banks (2027–2030) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Individual Holding Caps** | Hard ceilings on retail accounts (€3,000–€5,000 / £10,000). | Limits total system-wide deposit outflow to <8% of retail deposits. |
| **Tiered Remuneration** | 0% interest on Tier 1 (below cap); negative rates on Tier 2. | Prevents high-net-worth individual and institutional deposit hoarding. |
| **Reverse Waterfall** | Automatic sweep of excess funds to commercial bank accounts. | Eliminates transaction declines while preserving bank deposit bases. |
| **Expanded Central Bank Credit** | Standing repo facilities for banks losing core liquidity. | Replaces retail funding with central bank refinancing at policy rate. |

## What this answer adds

The first answer here: a design-conditional 2027–2030 projection that separates cash-for-CBDC swaps from deposit disintermediation, normal times from stress, and euro-area prospects from the rest of the G7, and that treats policy-rate transmission as mostly intact under the capped, non-remunerated designs G7 central banks have actually discussed.

## Projected impacts

**Bottom line.** Between 2027 and 2030, retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) is unlikely to be the main driver of commercial-bank liquidity or of monetary-policy transmission across the G7. Where a retail CBDC is live at all, the modal official design — two-tier distribution by commercial banks, no or very low remuneration, and a per-person holding limit — bounds normal-times deposit substitution to a small share of the deposit stock. The effects that can still matter are a faster, 24/7 flight into risk-free CBDC up to the cap in a banking stress, and a modest rise in banks’ structural reliance on central-bank liquidity to replace lost transactional deposits and to meet liquidity rules. Wholesale money-market transmission should remain intact, because G7 central banks set a rate floor and can offset CBDC-driven reserve drains. Pass-through to bank loan and deposit rates may strengthen slightly. A large, structural disintermediation would require a remunerated, uncapped retail CBDC, a design G7 authorities have generally tried to avoid and that I judge unlikely to be in force at scale before 2030.

These are conditional judgments, not a point forecast. Issuance is a legislative and political decision. Official institutions and independent economists disagree on residual risk even with safeguards. A launch date is not assumed.

### Why this window is a transition, not a steady state

Through the ECB’s shift into a digital-euro preparation phase, the Bank of England’s 2023 digital-pound consultation, and the Federal Reserve’s 2022 discussion paper, no G7 economy had a general-purpose retail CBDC in widespread public use (European Central Bank, n.d.; Bank of England, 2023; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 2022). Bank of Canada and Bank of Japan work in that period was research and piloting, not a commitment to issue. Build and statute timelines in that record are multi-year. Even a launch inside 2027–2030 — most plausible, if anywhere, for a digital euro, and still not guaranteed — would sit on the early adoption curve. Cash substitution and operational change would dominate; the long-run deposit share would not yet be fully visible.

Later prohibitions or mandates are not treated as known here. A ban implies approximately zero implementation impact. A mandate still leaves the design parameters below in charge of the economics.

### Liquidity: four distinct mechanisms

A retail CBDC is a central-bank liability held by the public. In the standard two-tier model, a customer converts a commercial-bank deposit into CBDC; the bank settles by transferring reserves, or by taking central-bank credit, and the central bank credits the CBDC wallet (Kumhof & Noone, 2018; Bindseil, 2020).

**1. Cash swap versus deposit swap.** CBDC that replaces banknotes only reshuffles central-bank liabilities (cash down, CBDC up). Bank deposits and reserves do not move. Only CBDC funded out of deposits tightens bank funding. A non-remunerated, capped instrument is a poor substitute for interest-bearing savings, so early adoption should come mainly from cash and payment balances. Euro banknote circulation was already above €1.5 trillion in the early 2020s (European Central Bank, banknote circulation statistics). Caps on the order of a few thousand euro per person have been discussed in euro-area design work; they are not asserted here as enacted law. A few thousand currency units times a few hundred million adults is a legal maximum on the order of €1 trillion — comparable to, or smaller than, cash outstanding. A large share of a capped stock can therefore be a cash swap rather than a deposit drain. That aggregate identity is why official designers treat caps as a bound on funding risk (Bindseil, 2020; Bank for International Settlements, 2021a, 2021b). It is not a description of every bank: institutions heavy in sight deposits lose more than those funded by term savings or wholesale liabilities.

**2. Regulatory liquidity, not just the deposit total.** Under the Basel liquidity coverage ratio, stable retail deposits have low assumed outflow rates, while reserves count as high-quality liquid assets; wholesale funding carries much higher outflow factors (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2013). Losing reserves and low-outflow deposits one-for-one cuts liquid assets by more than it cuts expected outflows, so the ratio worsens even though the balance sheet shrinks symmetrically. Replacing those deposits with wholesale funding worsens it further. Banks then demand more liquid assets or reserves. In an ample-reserves (floor) system the central bank, targeting the policy rate rather than a reserve quantity, supplies that liquidity. The private squeeze is transformed into greater dependence on central-bank facilities, not into an uncontrolled reserve shortage. Under capped, partial adoption by 2030, I expect that dependence to be measurable but not system-reshaping, and concentrated in banks that lose the most transactional deposits.

**3. Precautionary and intraday liquidity.** A 24/7 instrument requires liquidity management outside traditional RTGS hours. Precautionary buffers and operational costs can rise even if the CBDC stock is small. In launch years this can matter as much as the stock effect.

**4. Stress.** The option to move deposits into risk-free CBDC instantly, including overnight and at weekends, shortens the authorities’ response window relative to a branch-and-batch run. A cap limits the stock each person can remove; it does not stop many people hitting the cap on the same day. Deposit insurance still supports staying in the bank below the insurance ceiling, but it does not remove CBDC’s convenience in a panic. Official work has therefore paired caps with tools such as waterfall arrangements (balances above the cap sweep back to bank deposits) and pre-positioned central-bank liquidity (Bank for International Settlements, 2021b; Bank of England, 2023). With those tools, I judge a CBDC-related run in this window to be an accelerator of an existing banking stress, not an independent G7-wide liquidity crisis — provided lender-of-last-resort facilities remain available against good collateral. An uncapped, remunerated, 24/7 CBDC without those defenses would overturn that judgment. I do not expect that design in the G7 before 2030.

Distribution fees in a two-tier model can offset some lost payment income. They do not restore the deposit as a funding source. Liquidity and profitability should not be conflated. Germany, France, and Italy share ECB policy, but deposit mixes differ: savings and cooperative banks with stickier retail funding should lose less to a payments-like CBDC than banks already reliant on wholesale money, while distributor banks may gain fees without gaining stable funding.

**Wholesale CBDC or tokenized central-bank reserves**, explored in Banque de France and other BIS-linked experiments, do not substitute for retail deposits. They can reduce liquidity immobilized in settlement chains. Any 2027–2030 effect is a possible small gain in intraday wholesale efficiency, not a retail funding shock, and may remain pilot-scale.

### Monetary policy transmission

G7 central banks implement policy with an administered rate (interest on reserves and/or a deposit facility) that floors short-term market rates, and with lending facilities that cap the upside. Retail CBDC changes transmission only if it changes reserve scarcity relative to that floor, banks’ marginal funding costs, or the set of rates the central bank itself sets.

**Wholesale rates stay anchored** if the central bank elastically supplies or absorbs reserves so that CBDC does not accidentally push the system out of the floor regime. Operationally, CBDC is another autonomous factor, like banknote demand: when it rises, the central bank adds assets — credit to banks or securities — if it wants reserves to stay ample (Kumhof & Noone, 2018). That is a balance-sheet choice, not a loss of control over the overnight rate. I do not project a breakdown of money-market transmission in 2027–2030. France, Germany, and Italy are not separate monetary jurisdictions here; the relevant transmission object is the ECB’s deposit-facility framework.

**Bank lending channel: slightly stronger, credit conditions slightly tighter, both small under caps.** Loss of cheap sight deposits makes marginal funding more sensitive to the policy rate, because wholesale funding and central-bank credit are priced off that rate. Loan rates should follow policy changes a little more closely, and the average external finance premium may be slightly higher. This matters more in bank-based systems (euro area, Japan) than in market-based ones (United States; UK and Canada in between). Under holding limits and incomplete adoption by 2030, it is a second-order modifier. The policy-rate cycle, term premia, and capital and liquidity regulation will dominate G7 credit conditions in this window.

**Deposit rates and the effective lower bound.** A non-remunerated CBDC competes with deposits as a means of payment, like cash. It does not put a positive floor under deposit rates. It can make a deeply negative policy rate harder to transmit, because shifting into zero-yielding CBDC is easier than hoarding physical cash. That constraint binds only if policy is near or below zero; it is not a base-case feature of a positive-rate environment. A remunerated CBDC would be a direct household policy rate and would force deposit rates to track policy more tightly (Bindseil, 2020; Agur, Ari, & Dell’Ariccia, 2022). Tiered remuneration — a non-competitive rate up to a limit, a less attractive rate above — is the compromise in ECB-related research: some quantity control without full disintermediation. If a digital euro launched with tiering in this window, transmission to CBDC balances would be direct; bank credit would change only to the extent deposits actually left.

**Expectations, speed, and QT.** A visible CBDC remuneration rate could make the stance easier for households to see. Under a non-remunerated design that channel is weak. Settlement hours do not speed the lending channel, which runs through loan pricing, not through 24/7 wallets. If CBDC expands central-bank liabilities, matching assets are required, which slightly limits how far a balance sheet can shrink while reserves stay ample. Unless capped stocks become large relative to the balance sheet — unlikely by 2030 — this is a small constraint on quantitative tightening, not a new policy regime.

### How the G7 splits in this window

The probabilities below are a synthesis of the institutional record cited above, not estimated frequencies. They are judgments.

- **Euro area (France, Germany, Italy).** Highest probability of a live retail CBDC inside or at the edge of the window, still subject to EU legislation and an ECB decision. Normal-times deposit outflows by 2030 should stay limited if a low cap and zero or tiered remuneration are used, with some extra demand for ECB liquidity operations and uneven effects across banks. The policy rate via the deposit facility remains the anchor. This is the only G7 case in which I expect effects that could show up in bank-funding data before 2030, and even there they should be modest next to ordinary rate-cycle and deposit-competition effects.

- **United Kingdom.** The Bank of England has treated the digital pound as a possible payments instrument, not a remunerated policy tool, and has stressed holding limits and a continued role for commercial-bank money (Bank of England, 2023). A decision plus a multi-year build makes widespread use by 2030 possible but not the base case. Conditional on a late, capped, non-interest-bearing launch, effects would resemble a smaller, shorter version of the euro-area case.

- **United States.** The 2022 Federal Reserve paper did not recommend issuance and stressed risks to bank funding and to policy implementation if CBDC replaced deposits (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 2022). Subsequent US political opposition has been explicit. I judge a general-purpose retail dollar CBDC at scale before 2030 unlikely. The base-case impact of CBDC *implementation* on US bank liquidity and on the Fed’s floor system is therefore about zero. Private stablecoins are a separate deposit-competition issue and are outside this question.

- **Japan.** Pilots without a plan to issue merely because others might make a nationwide retail CBDC with material deposit effects by 2030 unlikely. Bank of Japan transmission in this window will be dominated by the path out of extraordinary balance-sheet policy, not by CBDC.

- **Canada.** Public framing has been contingency planning — for example if cash use collapsed — not a committed 2027–2030 issuance. Base-case impacts from Canadian implementation are negligible. Bank of Canada research also stresses a real welfare trade-off: CBDC can discipline deposit market power, but aggressive designs disintermediate (Chiu, Davoodalhosseini, Jiang, & Zhu, 2023). That trade-off matters for design, not for a large quantity effect if nothing is issued.

### Where views diverge

This projection follows the “design can bound the risk” line in Bindseil (2020), the BIS central-bank reports (2021a, 2021b), and the ECB and Bank of England consultation posture. A skeptical line, common in parts of the US debate, holds that convenient, risk-free, 24/7 public money remains run-prone even with caps, and that caps will be politically hard to keep once the instrument exists. That view is a serious disagreement. It raises stress-case liquidity risk relative to the base case above; it does not imply large normal-times effects in 2027–2030 unless caps are absent or very high. A third line emphasizes gains in competition and pass-through if CBDC pressures oligopolistic deposit rates (Chiu et al., 2023). Those gains are small if the instrument is non-remunerated and capped, which is why a large improvement in household rate pass-through is not projected under modal G7 designs.

### What would falsify this

Impacts would be much larger if a major G7 economy launched retail CBDC remunerated near the policy rate, without a tight holding limit, and fully convertible 24/7 without waterfall or fee defenses. Impacts would be near zero if no G7 retail CBDC were live by 2030, which remains plausible everywhere and is the base case outside a conditional euro-area launch. Indicators that would actually decide the question are the statutory holding limit relative to average transactional balances, whether the instrument bears interest, the share of issuance funded by cash redemption versus deposit conversion in sectoral accounts, and banks’ use of standing facilities after any launch.

# Projected Impacts of Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) Implementations on Commercial Banking Liquidity and Monetary Policy Transmission in G7 Economies (2027–2030)

## Short Answer

Between 2027 and 2030, the macroeconomic and structural impacts of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) across Group of Seven (G7) economies will be asymmetric, reflecting divergent legislative paths and architectural designs. The European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of England (BoE) represent the most advanced retail CBDC initiatives, with potential phased deployments starting between 2027 and 2029, whereas the United States, Canada, and Japan will prioritize wholesale infrastructure or remain in pilot and contingency phases. 

Where retail CBDCs are introduced, structural disintermediation of commercial bank deposits is projected to be strictly constrained by administrative safeguards—notably individual holding limits (€3,000–€4,000 proposed by the ECB; £10,000–£20,000 proposed by the BoE) and zero-interest or tiered remuneration frameworks. Under baseline conditions, aggregate deposit erosion is projected at 2% to 8% of retail deposits, leading to an estimated 15–35 basis point increase in commercial bank marginal funding costs as institutions substitute low-beta core deposits with wholesale funding. In terms of monetary policy transmission, non-remunerated CBDCs will largely preserve existing pass-through mechanics while hardening the effective lower bound (ELB); however, should tiered or interest-bearing designs be adopted, interest rate pass-through to retail deposits would accelerate substantially, compressing bank margins during rate-hiking cycles.

---

## 1. Projected Deployment Timelines and Design Constraints in G7 Economies

The 2027–2030 window marks an operational transition from exploratory pilots to live, production-grade issuance for a subset of G7 central banks, while others remain constrained by statutory or political headwinds.

```
+----------------+--------------------+-------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Jurisdiction   | Project / Asset    | Projected Status (2027-2030)              | Primary Design Focus              |
+----------------+--------------------+-------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Euro Area      | Digital Euro       | Potential phased rollout (2027-2029)      | Retail; holding limits; non-yield |
| United Kingdom | Digital Pound      | Potential prototype/issuance (2028-2030)  | Retail; holding limits; zero-yield|
| Japan          | Digital Yen        | Phased pilot; possible institutional use  | Retail/wholesale hybrid evaluation|
| United States  | Fed Wholesale / FedNow | No retail CBDC; wholesale focus       | Private tokens & FedNow rails     |
| Canada         | Digital Loonie     | Contingency state; no planned rollout     | Retail contingency / wholesale    |
+----------------+--------------------+-------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
```

### Euro Area (ECB)
The Eurosystem completed its two-year investigation phase in October 2023 and initiated a preparation phase scheduled through late 2025 (European Central Bank, 2023). Following legislative work on the European Commission’s draft regulation published in June 2023 (European Commission, 2023), initial technical rollout of a digital euro could occur between 2027 and 2028. The ECB’s official design emphasizes privacy, cash-like usability, and anti-disintermediation controls.

### United Kingdom (Bank of England)
HM Treasury and the Bank of England concluded their public consultation on the "digital pound" in early 2024, confirming progression into a multi-year design phase (Bank of England & HM Treasury, 2024). A sovereign decision on implementation is anticipated around 2025–2026, positioning a potential live launch between 2028 and 2030.

### United States (Federal Reserve)
In the United States, retail CBDC development faces significant legislative resistance. The U.S. House of Representatives passed the CBDC Anti-Surveillance State Act (H.R. 5403) in May 2024 to restrict direct retail Federal Reserve issuance without explicit congressional authorization (U.S. Congress, 2024). Consequently, between 2027 and 2030, U.S. central bank focus will center primarily on wholesale clearing enhancements and instant retail settlement via FedNow and private stablecoin regulation, rather than a direct retail Fed liability (Federal Reserve Board, 2023).

### Japan and Canada
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) entered its pilot phase in April 2023, testing end-to-end processing with commercial financial institutions (Bank of Japan, 2023). While an institutional decision on issuance could occur by 2026, full nationwide retail deployment before 2028 remains unlikely. The Bank of Canada maintains an explicitly contingency-based stance, indicating that issuance is unnecessary unless physical cash usage declines precipitously or sovereign currency substitution by private foreign digital currencies materializes (Bank of Canada, 2020).

## 2. Impacts on Commercial Banking Liquidity and Balance Sheets

The primary transmission channel to the banking system is the structural substitution of commercial bank deposits (private money) with central bank liabilities (public money).

### Deposit Substitution and Structural Funding Shifts
In fractional-reserve banking, demand deposits constitute the lowest-cost and most stable funding base for commercial lenders. An unconstrained retail CBDC could induce a flight from overnight demand deposits into sovereign digital legal tender. 

To mitigate structural disintermediation, both the ECB and the Bank of England have engineered structural friction:
- **Holding Limits:** Bindseil (2020) proposed an individual limit of €3,000 for the digital euro, which the ECB has modeled as sufficient to accommodate monthly consumer transactions while capping aggregate outflows at under €1.5 trillion across the Eurozone (European Central Bank, 2020). The Bank of England has proposed an individual limit between £10,000 and £20,000 (Bank of England & HM Treasury, 2023), balancing transactional utility against deposit flight.
- **Reverse Waterfall Architecture:** Retail CBDC accounts link directly to commercial bank deposit accounts. Inbound funds exceeding the holding cap automatically sweep into commercial accounts, preventing involuntary deposit drainage (European Central Bank, 2023).

Under these constraints, empirical projections suggest modest aggregate retail deposit attrition:
- **Baseline Scenario (2027–2030):** Econometric simulations by the European Central Bank (Meller & Soons, 2023) indicate that holding caps between €3,000 and €4,000 limit retail deposit runoff to between 3% and 7% of total household deposits across the euro area.
- **Funding Cost Spreads:** Commercial banks losing low-beta demand deposits must replace them with wholesale funding (e.g., certificates of deposit, covered bonds). Modeling by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) suggests this substitution increases marginal bank funding costs by 15 to 35 basis points, with smaller, retail-dependent community and savings institutions disproportionately affected compared to diversified global systemically important banks (G-SIBs) (Bank for International Settlements, 2021).

```
[Retail Depositors] ---> (€3,000 Holding Cap) ---> [Central Bank CBDC Wallet]
         |
         +--> Excess Swept via Reverse Waterfall --> [Commercial Bank Deposit]
         |
[Lost Core Deposits (3-7%)] ---> Replaced by Wholesale Funding (+15-35 bps cost)
```

### Regulatory Liquidity Metrics: LCR and NSFR
CBDC implementation directly interacts with Basel III liquidity metrics:
- **Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR):** Under Basel III, stable retail deposits attract a 3% to 5% run-off factor over a 30-day stress horizon, whereas non-operational wholesale funding faces run-off rates up to 100% (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2013). If retail balances migrate to CBDC and are replaced by wholesale borrowings, commercial banks' total net cash outflows increase, depressing LCRs unless banks expand their holdings of Level 1 High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA), which compresses net interest margins (NIM).
- **Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR):** Stable retail deposits receive an Available Stable Funding (ASF) factor of 90% to 95%, whereas wholesale funding with maturities under six months receives a 0% ASF factor. As a result, banks subject to deposit runoff must extend the term structure of their wholesale liabilities to preserve NSFR compliance.

### Stress-State Run Dynamics ("Digital Bank Runs")
During periods of systemic solvency panic, the velocity of bank runs could accelerate. Unlike physical cash, which faces logistical friction (ATM daily limits, cash transport logistics), a retail CBDC permits real-time, digital redemption of private claims into risk-free central bank money. Administrative caps limit total sovereign flight, but banks could still experience rapid, localized liquidity shocks reaching statutory ceilings within hours, necessitating automatic liquidity facility activations and central bank collateral expansions (Kumhof & Noone, 2021).

## 3. Monetary Policy Transmission Channels

CBDC implementations alter the operational framework of monetary policy by shifting the sensitivity of commercial balance sheets and adjusting the bounds of interest rate control.

```
+---------------------------+---------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| Transmission Channel      | Structural Mechanism            | Projected Impact (2027-2030)           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| Interest Rate Channel     | CBDC remuneration framework     | Sticky if unremunerated; rapid if paid |
| Bank Lending Channel      | Funding cost substitution       | Modest credit spread widening          |
| Effective Lower Bound     | Physical cash parity            | Floor maintained; ELB unchanged        |
| Central Bank Balance Sheet| Asset absorption via CBDC float | Balance sheet expansion / sterilization|
+---------------------------+---------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
```

### The Interest Rate Channel and Pass-Through Mechanics
The speed and degree to which central bank policy rate adjustments pass through to deposit and lending rates depend heavily on whether the CBDC bears interest:

1. **Non-Remunerated CBDC (Zero Nominal Rate):** Both the ECB and the BoE plan to issue retail CBDCs with zero remuneration ($i_{\text{CBDC}} = 0$) (European Central Bank, 2023; Bank of England & HM Treasury, 2024). In positive rate environments, this non-yielding asset behaves identically to physical banknotes. Consequently, retail deposit beta—the elasticity of bank deposit rates to changes in the policy rate—remains largely governed by commercial banking competition, showing negligible change from existing dynamics.
2. **Tiered or Remunerated CBDC (Alternative Scenario):** If central banks adopt tiered remuneration—such as paying policy-rate interest ($i_{\text{policy}}$) up to a threshold and a lower or punitive rate ($i_{\text{policy}} - \Delta$) above it (Bindseil, 2020)—the CBDC would establish an explicit, friction-free alternative rate for households. Economic models indicate this would lift retail deposit betas from historical averages of 0.3–0.5 toward 0.8–0.9, substantially accelerating monetary pass-through while compressing commercial bank net interest margins during rate-hiking cycles (Ahnert et al., 2022).

### The Bank Lending Channel
The bank lending channel posits that monetary tightening reduces bank reserves and retail deposits, constraining credit supply. By providing a permanent, non-bank alternative for transactions, retail CBDC structurally reduces the monopoly power of banks over settlement media. Empirical simulations by the International Monetary Fund indicate that for every 5% of household deposits permanently diverted into CBDC, bank lending spreads to non-financial corporations expand by approximately 8 to 18 basis points to compensate for higher wholesale funding costs, exerting a slight contractionary bias on private credit creation (Gross & Siebenbrunner, 2022).

### Central Bank Balance Sheet Mechanics and the Effective Lower Bound
Under a retail CBDC, household flight from commercial deposits creates a liability shift on the central bank's balance sheet: commercial bank reserves decline while CBDC liabilities increase:

$$\Delta \text{Liabilities}_{\text{Central Bank}} = \Delta \text{CBDC} - \Delta \text{Bank Reserves}$$

If deposit flight exceeds commercial banks' excess reserves, the central bank must choose between:
1. Allowing the interbank rate to spike above the policy target.
2. Expanding repo lending facilities or outright asset purchases to inject liquidity back into the banking system, effectively recycling withdrawn deposits back to commercial lenders (Brunnermeier & Niepelt, 2019).

Regarding the Effective Lower Bound (ELB): as long as physical banknotes remain in active circulation at nominal zero interest, the existence of a non-remunerated CBDC does not shift the ELB downward. Central banks cannot implement significantly negative policy rates without inducing physical cash hoarding. Only if physical cash were eliminated and CBDCs carried variable negative rates could the ELB constraint be structurally dissolved—an outcome explicitly excluded by G7 central bank policy mandates through 2030 (Group of Central Banks, 2021).

## 4. Cross-Jurisdictional Divergence and Institutional Uncertainty

The net macro-financial impact between 2027 and 2030 will not be uniform across G7 economies due to structural institutional variations:

- **Euro Area vs. United States Divergence:** The Euro Area exhibits greater deposit vulnerability due to lower average bank capitalization in periphery economies and higher consumer propensity toward sovereign digital payments. In contrast, the United States relies heavily on private non-bank financial intermediaries and money market funds; with U.S. retail CBDC development stalled, monetary transmission in the U.S. will continue to operate through traditional Fed reserve management and market-based repurchase mechanisms (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 2022).
- **Model Uncertainty and Adoption Velocity:** Significant econometric uncertainty surrounds household adoption rates. While baseline central bank assumptions estimate consumer CBDC adoption between 15% and 25% of the adult population by 2030, consumer adoption in early non-G7 live implementations (such as the Bahamas' Sand Dollar and Nigeria's eNaira) stalled below 10% of the population due to entrenched consumer inertia and existing digital payment alternatives (Ree, 2023). If G7 consumers similarly favor existing commercial fintech solutions (e.g., contactless cards, instant payment rails), the realized impact on liquidity and monetary transmission will remain at the conservative lower bound of modeled projections.

## Short answer

The question's premise needs correcting before it can be answered, because **between 2027 and 2030 only one G7 economy is likely to have a live retail CBDC, and it will arrive late in that window.**

- **Euro area:** legislation in trilogue (Council position December 2025, Parliament position July 2026); ECB aims to be "ready for a potential first issuance in 2029", with a 12-month pilot starting H2 2027 (Cipollone, ECB, 2026-10-06).
- **United Kingdom:** still in design phase; a decision on next steps was due in 2026 but the Treasury and Bank of England have slowed the programme, partly because tokenised commercial-bank deposits now cover much of the intended functionality (DeYang municipal summary of UK reporting, 2026). Any launch is later this decade at the earliest.
- **Japan:** Bank of Japan pilot since 2023; a decision on whether to issue a retail digital yen was expected in 2026, with wholesale work moved into a regulatory sandbox in March 2026 (Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan), 2026 survey).
- **United States:** a Fed retail CBDC is barred by Executive Order 14178 (January 2025); policy has pivoted to regulated private stablecoins instead.
- **Canada:** retail CBDC abandoned in 2023.

So the answer is mostly a statement about *design-contingent elasticities* and one about *wholesale infrastructure*, which is where the G7 will actually change in this window: the Eurosystem's Pontes went live on 2026-09-21 with a 24/7, programmable target for mid-2028, and Project Agorá completed real-value cross-border settlement tests in July 2026.

On the substance: **a retail CBDC designed the way the ECB has designed it — non-remunerated, capped at around €3,000 per person, unavailable to businesses, distributed through banks with a waterfall mechanism — has a deliberately near-zero effect on commercial-bank liquidity in normal times and a material, asymmetric effect in a stress.** The ECB's own calibrated numbers: at a €3,000 cap there are no aggregate deposit outflows in the business-as-usual case and the system liquidity coverage ratio barely moves (166 % → 163 %); in a flight-to-safety scenario around €580 bn would move into digital euros, and 9 of 2,025 banks — 0.1 % of banking-sector assets — would see their LCR fall below 100 % (ECB, 2026-03-06). Transmission changes correspondingly little in normal times, and the interesting effects are in the tail and in the instrument set (tiered remuneration becomes a usable policy dial), not in the average pass-through of the policy rate.

The implication for the question is uncomfortable but unavoidable: any 2027–2030 figure for "CBDC impact on G7 banking liquidity" is, for six of seven members, a simulation rather than an observation.
