Between 2027 and 2030, CBDCs in the G7 will most likely reshape commercial bank liquidity at the margin rather than displace it, while giving central banks a sharper but narrower monetary transmission channel. The reason is timing and design: within the window, only the euro area is on a credible path to a live retail CBDC, and it will launch capped, non-interest-bearing, and intermediated through banks. The liquidity risk is therefore real but bounded in normal times, and concentrated in stress episodes; the transmission gain comes less from a new policy rate on CBDC than from programmable settlement, faster pass-through to payment balances, and better data on money flows.

**Where the G7 actually stands**

The euro area is the only G7 jurisdiction with a dated launch path. The European Central Bank plans a 12-month internal pilot beginning in the second half of 2027, involving 36 selected payment service providers, and aims to be ready for a possible first issuance in 2029, conditional on EU legislation being adopted by the end of 2026 (European Central Bank, 2025, 2026). The United Kingdom is a step behind: the Bank of England and HM Treasury remain in a design phase, with a decision on next steps due by the end of 2026 and no issuance date set; if a build decision were taken, issuance would not follow until the second half of the decade at the earliest (Bank of England & HM Treasury, 2023, 2024, 2026). The United States has no live retail CBDC programme and the Federal Reserve has not recommended one, while Japan and Canada continue pilot and research work without firm launch dates. The practical consequence is that, for 2027-2030, CBDC effects on G7 banking will be dominated by one system — the euro area — with the rest of the G7 experiencing preparatory and wholesale-settlement effects only.

**Liquidity: slow disintermediation in calm times, fast disintermediation in stress**

The central mechanism is substitution. A retail CBDC is a direct liability of the central bank, and therefore a close substitute for a commercial bank deposit — or, if interest-bearing, a near-perfect one. When households shift balances into CBDC, banks lose low-cost retail funding and must replace it with wholesale borrowing, central bank borrowing, or higher deposit rates, which raises funding costs and can reduce credit availability or raise its price (Bidder, Jackson, & Rottner, 2025).

Research from the Bank for International Settlements distinguishes two speeds of this effect. "Slow disintermediation" is the steady drain of deposits in normal times as households hold some CBDC for payments. "Fast disintermediation" is the run risk: in distress, a CBDC offers storage at scale, unlike cash, so depositors can flee to risk-free central bank money instantly and in large volumes, accelerating digital runs (Bidder, Jackson, & Rottner, 2025). The same study finds that a suitably designed CBDC — in particular one with holding limits — can choke off the fast channel and, by shrinking a fragile banking system, actually enhance financial stability.

For 2027-2030 this implies a two-part liquidity outlook. In normal conditions, the deposit drain should be modest: the digital euro is designed as a payment instrument, not a store of value, with per-person holding limits and no remuneration, so most balances will stay in bank accounts and the CBDC will mainly substitute for cash and card payments rather than deposits. In stress conditions, however, the run channel is genuinely new, and its containment depends entirely on whether the holding limits and any tiered remuneration hold up under political pressure during a crisis — the moment when raising limits looks most tempting and is most dangerous. Banks should therefore expect somewhat higher structural funding costs and a need for larger liquidity buffers, rather than a sudden loss of their deposit base.

**Monetary policy transmission: sharper at the edges, not transformed**

CBDCs affect transmission through three channels. First, if the CBDC is remunerated, its rate becomes a direct policy instrument that reaches households without passing through bank deposit rates — but the G7 designs in prospect are non-interest-bearing, so this channel will be largely absent before 2030. Second, CBDC settlement infrastructure shortens payment lags and makes the stock of central bank money held by the public observable in near-real time, improving the central bank's read on money demand and the speed at which policy-rate changes reach payment balances. Third, and most consequentially, a CBDC changes the transmission of tightening: when deposits can flee to CBDC, banks facing outflows must raise deposit rates faster to retain funding, which can actually strengthen the pass-through of rate hikes to savers — but it also makes bank funding more flighty, so the same mechanism can amplify a credit contraction if outflows accelerate.

The net effect is asymmetric. In easing cycles, CBDCs add little, because a non-remunerated CBDC cannot carry a negative policy rate to households and banks still intermediate credit. In tightening cycles and in stress, CBDCs make transmission faster and more volatile: policy reaches deposit pricing more quickly, but the banking system's funding becomes more sensitive to confidence shocks. Central banks will therefore gain a finer instrument for steering payment-system liquidity while losing some of the stickiness that made bank deposits a stable funding base — a trade-off that argues for keeping CBDC holdings capped and for expanding standing liquidity facilities so that banks can replace lost retail funding at predictable terms.

**What banks and policymakers should do before 2030**

Banks in the euro area should treat the 2027 pilot as the start of a real funding-mix shift: reprice deposit franchises on the assumption that a share of transactional balances migrates, build wholesale funding capacity, and stress-test deposit outflows that are faster than any historical run, because the CBDC rail removes the physical friction of withdrawing cash. Policymakers should lock in holding limits and tiered remuneration in legislation before launch, not leave them as adjustable parameters, and should pre-commit liquidity backstops so that a CBDC-induced outflow does not force fire sales. For the rest of the G7, the priority is different: use the window to settle the design questions — interest-bearing or not, caps or not, bank-intermediated or direct — because the choices made now determine whether a CBDC launched after 2030 becomes a payment utility or a systemic funding shock.

## Verdict / Executive Summary

Between 2027 and 2030, no G7 economy is projected to operate a full-scale retail CBDC at scale, so the aggregate impact on commercial banking liquidity and monetary policy transmission in that window is likely to be small and design-contingent rather than structural [S1][S2]. Where CBDCs do launch, the dominant modeled risk is deposit outflow ("disintermediation") whose magnitude spans roughly 0–37% of retail deposits depending entirely on holding limits and remuneration; and monetary policy transmission is projected to shift from a bank-lending channel toward a more direct central-bank-to-public rate channel, with the sign of the effect depending on whether the CBDC is interest-bearing [S3][S4][S5]. I cannot confirm the "24–37%" figure cited in Answer 1 from a source I was able to open, and I flag that below rather than repeat it as fact.

## What this Answer adds beyond earlier verified Answers

1. **A dated, country-by-country status check for the G7 as of late 2025/2026** — which of the seven have legislated, piloted, deferred, or cancelled a retail CBDC — because the 2027–2030 impact is bounded by what actually launches. Earlier Answers asserted "developmental or limited-pilot phases" generically without naming jurisdictions or the cancellations (notably Canada's retail CBDC work being wound down and the US digital dollar paused by executive order) [S1][S6][S7].
2. **A correction/qualification to Answer 1's "24–37% deposit displacement" figure**: I could not open a source that states this range. The comparable, verifiable BIS/BoE-adjacent estimates I can confirm are of a different order under realistic designs (single-digit percent of deposits under capped designs; larger only under uncapped, remunerated designs) [S3][S5]. I state the uncertainty rather than repeat an unconfirmable number.
3. **A quantified transmission mechanism**: the interest-rate pass-through equation for a remunerated CBDC as an explicit policy-rate floor, and the balance-sheet identity showing how deposit outflow raises funding costs — mechanisms earlier Answers asserted only as conclusions [S4][S8].
4. **Explicit residual uncertainty**: no published G7 central bank has issued a point forecast for 2027–2030 liquidity impact; all figures are model outputs under stated assumptions, not projections with confidence intervals.

## Reasoning and evidence

**Step 1 — What actually launches by 2030 (scope boundary).**
The question asks about impacts "between 2027 and 2030." Impact requires implementation. As of the most recent BIS survey I can confirm, most G7 central banks are in research/pilot, not production:

- **Eurozone (ECB):** digital euro in "preparation phase" since Nov 2023; no legislative adoption of the regulation as of the latest ECB statements I can confirm; ECB has stated a launch decision would be followed by multi-year build-out [S1][S2].
- **United States:** retail digital dollar effectively paused — the July 2025 executive order terminated work on a US CBDC and directed agencies to end related efforts [S7]. So US impact in 2027–2030 ≈ 0 for a retail CBDC.
- **Canada:** the Bank of Canada ended its retail CBDC (Digital Canadian Dollar) engagement work in 2024–2025 as the government shifted priority to stablecoins [S6]. Impact ≈ 0 unless reversed.
- **United Kingdom:** Bank of England and HM Treasury advanced a digital pound to a "design phase" (Feb 2025 consultation), with a decision on issuance not expected before the late 2020s [S1]. Launch before 2030 is possible but not committed.
- **Japan:** Bank of Japan running a pilot since 2023; no issuance decision; BOJ officials have publicly said a yen CBDC decision is not imminent [S1].
- **Germany/France/Italy:** covered under the digital euro track above.
- **Uncertainty:** I cannot confirm the precise current (Nov 2026) status of each of these beyond what BIS/ECB/BoE pages I could open state; status may have moved. Treat this as a snapshot, not a forecast.

**Inference:** For at most the euro area and possibly the UK, a retail CBDC could be live in some limited form within 2027–2030; for the US and Canada, effectively not. Therefore the G7-wide liquidity impact in the window is bounded by the euro-area/UK case only.

**Step 2 — Liquidity mechanism (quantified).**
Commercial bank consolidated balance sheet identity:

Assets = Loans + Reserves; Liabilities = Deposits + Wholesale funding + Equity.

If households move amount ΔD from deposits to CBDC, and the central bank does not sterilize, banks lose ΔD of stable funding. To keep lending constant they must raise ΔD of wholesale funding at a spread *s* over the deposit rate. Marginal cost of funds rises, so:

ΔNIM ≈ −(ΔD / Earning assets) × s, where s = wholesale–deposit spread.

Direction is unambiguous: outflow raises funding cost and compresses net interest margin unless offset. The **magnitude** is the contested part:

- Under **capped, non-remunerated** designs (the design the ECB has signalled: no interest on holdings, possible holding limits), published estimates put deposit displacement in the **low single-digit percent** of household deposits [S3][S5].
- Under **uncapped, remunerated** designs, model estimates rise substantially — some models produce displacement in the tens-of-percent range — but this is a model output under an assumption G7 central banks have explicitly said they do not intend to adopt [S3][S4].
- **Uncertainty:** I could not open a source confirming Answer 1's specific "24–37%" range; I therefore do not adopt it. The honest statement is: displacement ranges from near-zero under capped designs to potentially double-digit percentages under uncapped remunerated designs, with no G7 central bank publishing a point estimate for 2027–2030.

**Step 3 — Monetary policy transmission mechanism (quantified).**
Two channels:

(a) *Rate floor / direct channel.* If the CBDC pays interest r_C, then no retail deposit can sustainably offer below r_C minus a convenience adjustment, so the policy rate passes to retail rates with coefficient approaching 1 on the CBDC leg:

∂r_retail / ∂i_policy → 1 as CBDC holdings grow, if r_C is indexed to i_policy.

This strengthens pass-through but also **hardens the effective lower bound**: the central bank cannot cut r_C below ~0 without inducing a run from banks to CBDC (a "reversal rate" problem) [S4][S8].

(b) *Bank lending channel.* If deposits shrink by ΔD, credit supply contracts by roughly ΔD × (1 − reserve-ratio) in a simple multiplier, weakening the bank-lending channel of transmission [S4].

Net effect is **ambiguous in sign and depends on design**: remuneration strengthens (a) but weakens (b); caps and non-remuneration preserve (b) but give up (a). No G7 central bank has published a quantitative forecast of the net effect for 2027–2030.

**Step 4 — Synthesis for 2027–2030.**
Given Step 1 (limited launch), Step 2 (small displacement under intended designs), and Step 3 (design-contingent sign), the defensible projection is: **small, localized, design-contingent effects concentrated in the euro area (and possibly the UK), with no measurable G7-wide shift in monetary policy transmission in the window**, unless a G7 jurisdiction adopts an uncapped, remunerated design — which current policy statements do not indicate.

## Counter-arguments and boundary conditions

- **Falsifier 1:** If the ECB launches the digital euro with no holding cap and with remuneration above zero by 2028, my "low single-digit displacement" claim fails and Answer 1's larger figures become more plausible.
- **Falsifier 2:** If the US reverses the 2025 executive order and launches a digital dollar by 2029, my "US impact ≈ 0" claim fails.
- **Falsifier 3:** If a G7 central bank publishes a point forecast of deposit outflow for 2027–2030, my statement that "no G7 central bank has published a point estimate" fails.
- **Boundary:** This answer addresses *retail* CBDCs. Wholesale CBDC (e.g., for interbank settlement) has a different and generally smaller impact on retail deposit liquidity; if the question intended wholesale CBDC, the analysis would need to be redone.
- **Residual uncertainty I cannot resolve:** the actual launch dates and design parameters for the digital euro and digital pound as of Nov 2026 — my status snapshot may be stale, and I could not confirm post-2025 legislative developments beyond what the cited pages state.

## Short answer

The previous answers analyse CBDC as if a G7 retail CBDC were coming. As of November 2026, the decisive fact is the opposite: **almost no G7 retail CBDC will exist at scale during 2027–2030**. The United States has banned one by executive order, Canada has abandoned its retail programme, the UK has taken no decision to issue, and the digital euro — the only live G7 retail project — reaches pilot in late 2027 and first issuance only in 2029 at the earliest, capped and non-remunerated. The projected systemic impacts on bank liquidity and monetary transmission in the window are therefore **small by construction**. The impacts that do occur are: (i) a bounded, capped outflow in the euro area around the 2029 launch; (ii) near-term compliance and investment costs for euro-area banks before any CBDC exists; and (iii) the *substitute* shock — regulated stablecoins in the US doing the disintermediation work the literature attributes to CBDC. Two claims in the previous answers need correcting: the "24–37% deposit displacement" figure describes an unconstrained design no G7 authority proposes, and the "CBDC as a floor for deposit rates" mechanism requires a remunerated CBDC, which no G7 design proposes either.

## 2. Liquidity: the euro-area case is bounded by design, and the bound is small

The previous answers' core mechanism is right in direction and wrong in magnitude. Deposit substitution is real: when a household moves funds into a CBDC wallet, its bank loses reserves one-for-one, and the bank must replace cheap retail funding with wholesale funding or central-bank credit, compressing net interest margins and degrading LCR/NSFR (Infante et al., 2023). But every G7 design neutralises this by construction:

- **Holding limit.** The digital euro will be capped; the ECB has modelled limits of €500–€3,000 per person (Executive Board member Piero Cipollone, 6 October 2026) and the figure is still not fixed in law. Arithmetic upper bound: even if every euro-area resident (roughly 350 million people) held the maximum €3,000, total CBDC outstanding could not exceed ~€1 trillion — and that extreme is nobody's forecast. The ECB's own modelling concludes that at limits up to €3,000, realistic outflows are *outweighed* by an estimated €127 billion in additional bank deposits by 2034 from the shift away from cash (Cipollone, 6 October 2026). In other words, on the ECB's numbers the digital euro is roughly deposit-neutral for banks over the medium term.
- **Non-remuneration.** The ECB states plainly that, as with cash, no interest would be paid on digital euro holdings. A zero-yield instrument capped at €3,000 competes with a current account for *payments*, not with a savings deposit as a store of value — which is why take-up, not the cap alone, limits outflows.
- **Waterfall design.** Amounts above the cap sweep automatically into the holder's ordinary bank account, so the cap cannot be circumvented by accumulation and the funds never leave the banking system.

Against this, Answer 1's headline figure — Brühl (2026) estimating refinancing needs up to €650 billion for a digital euro — must be read as an **upper-bound, high-substitution scenario**, not a central case: it assumes substitution at a scale the cap, the zero yield and the waterfall are specifically designed to prevent. Answer 2's "24–37% of deposits displaced" is likewise an *unconstrained-design* result from the literature; it describes no G7 design actually proposed and should not be quoted as a 2027–2030 projection. The honest central case for euro-area banks in 2027–2030 is: modest deposit migration during the pilot and early issuance, concentrated in transaction balances, with funding costs rising slightly at the margin — and, importantly, **real costs before any launch at all**: the ECB's preparation-phase closing report puts development costs at ~€1.3 billion to first issuance, annual operating costs at ~€320 million from 2029, and banking-sector investment at €4–5.8 billion. Banks pay billions to build a system whose liquidity impact is designed to be small.

**Run risk.** The answers warn of frictionless digital bank runs into CBDC in a crisis. With a €3,000 cap, non-remuneration and the waterfall, the run channel is capped at €3,000 per person — a household can already withdraw far more than that in cash or by instant transfer today. The residual run risk in 2027–2030 is operational (pilot outages, wallet failures), not systemic. Note the irony: the instant, uncapped, 24/7 flight-to-safety instrument already exists — it is the US dollar stablecoin, not a CBDC.

## 3. Monetary policy transmission: the textbook channels mostly do not activate

- **Interest-rate channel.** Answers 2 and 3 argue a CBDC could harden the deposit-rate floor or sharpen pass-through. That mechanism requires a *remunerated* CBDC whose rate the central bank sets. No G7 design remunerates: the digital euro pays zero, and the US and Canada have no CBDC at all. With a non-remunerated, capped CBDC, the deposit-rate floor is unchanged and pass-through in 2027–2030 is unaffected. The Infante et al. (2023) result the answers cite — a sovereign outside option disciplining banks' market power over depositors — is correct as economics, but in 2027–2030 the outside option doing that work in the US is the regulated stablecoin, and in the euro area it is a €3,000-capped payment wallet, i.e. a weak version of it.
- **Bank lending channel.** If deposits did migrate at scale, the lending channel would weaken as banks' balance sheets shrank and the central bank dealt directly with the public. Per §2, migration is capped, so this channel is intact in the window. The one real change is on the central bank's own balance sheet: CBDC liabilities must be recycled (Infante et al., 2023) — via asset purchases or lending facilities back to banks — and the ECB will have to manage that recycling from 2029. Before then, the operational question is reserve forecasting: volatile CBDC demand complicates liquidity forecasting, but only once issuance begins.
- **Effective lower bound.** A non-remunerated CBDC replicates the zero lower bound of cash; it does not relax it. Negative-rate CBDC is ruled out in every G7 framework on political and legal grounds, as Answer 1 correctly notes.

## 4. The shock that actually arrives in 2027–2030 is not CBDC — it is tokenisation plus stablecoins

- **Wholesale CBDC and tokenised deposits.** While retail CBDC stalled, wholesale work accelerated: the BIS Project Agorá (launched 2024, seven central banks including the Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan, Bank of England and ECB, plus 40+ private financial firms) is prototyping tokenised cross-border settlement with wholesale CBDC and tokenised commercial-bank deposits on a shared ledger. For G7 banks in 2027–2030, the material change to liquidity management is 24/7 atomic settlement and programmability in wholesale markets — which compresses intraday liquidity needs and settlement risk — not retail deposit migration.
- **Stablecoins as the realised outside option.** In the US, the GENIUS Act's regulated stablecoins are the instrument households and firms actually use as a sovereign-adjacent digital dollar. Every disintermediation mechanism the CBDC literature models — deposit substitution, faster pass-through, flight to safety — is already operating through stablecoins, uncapped and 24/7. Any 2027–2030 forecast of bank liquidity that models CBDC but ignores stablecoins misattributes the shock. The policy-relevant question for G7 banks is therefore not "what if a CBDC launches" but "how fast do regulated stablecoins and tokenised deposits take transaction balances" — a question the previous answers do not ask.

## 5. What would change this forecast

(1) EU legislation slipping past end-2026 pushes digital euro issuance beyond 2029, shrinking even the euro-area impact to a pilot. (2) A change of US administration after 2028 reviving a digital dollar — the EO ban is reversible by a future president, though the GENIUS framework makes it less likely. (3) A financial crisis in the window forcing emergency issuance or a rapid flight into the capped wallet — the cap makes this a payments event, not a solvency event. (4) Stablecoin growth disintermediating transaction deposits faster than modelled — the most likely upside surprise to bank funding costs, and it requires no CBDC at all.

# Projected Impacts of CBDC Implementations on Commercial Banking Liquidity and Monetary Policy Transmission in G7 Economies (2027–2030)

## Executive Summary & Analytical Framework

Between 2027 and 2030, the introduction of retail Central Bank Digital Currencies (rCBDCs) across G7 economies will mark a structural shift in monetary architecture. While no G7 nation has committed to an unrestricted, fully unconstrained public deployment, central bank timelines—most notably the European Central Bank’s (ECB) preparation phase ending in late 2025/2027 and the Bank of England’s (BoE) design phase extending toward 2028—place potential initial operational rollouts squarely within the 2027–2030 window (European Central Bank, 2023; Bank of England, 2024). 

The economic transmission of an rCBDC operates primarily through the reallocation of liability structures across central bank and commercial bank balance sheets. Evaluating these impacts requires examining two core domains:
1. **Commercial Banking Liquidity:** The structural substitution of commercial bank deposits for risk-free central bank liabilities, its downstream effects on regulatory liquidity metrics (such as Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio [LCR] and Net Stable Funding Ratio [NSFR]), wholesale funding reliance, and financial-stress run velocity.
2. **Monetary Policy Transmission:** The realignment of deposit pricing power (deposit betas), interest rate pass-through dynamics, the operational enforcement of the Effective Lower Bound (ELB), and central bank balance sheet recycling mechanisms.

```
       [ Central Bank Balance Sheet ]                 [ Commercial Bank Balance Sheet ]
  +-------------------------------------+        +----------------------------------------+
  | Assets:             Liabilities:    |        | Assets:                Liabilities:    |
  | - Gov Bonds         - Reserves      |        | - Reserves (HQLA)      - Retail Deposits|
  | - Repo Loans        - Cash / rCBDC  |<-------| - Loans / Illiquid     - Wholesale Debt |
  +-------------------------------------+        |   Assets               - Equity         |
                                   ^             +----------------------------------------+
                                   |                                  |
                           (rCBDC Inflows)                   (Deposit Outflows)
                                   |                                  v
                        [ Household / Corporate CBDC Wallets ]
```

---

## 1. Structural Impacts on Commercial Banking Liquidity

### A. Deposit Disintermediation and Capital Structure Shifts
Retail commercial bank deposits represent uncollateralized, low-beta, stable liabilities for private banks. When households convert commercial deposits into rCBDCs, bank balance sheets experience a simultaneous drain of reserves (assets) and retail deposits (liabilities). 

*   **Substitution Elasticity:** Econometric modeling from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Federal Reserve indicates that without structural safeguards, an unconstrained, non-remunerated rCBDC could displace between 15% and 30% of commercial retail deposits under normal economic conditions (Ahnert et al., 2022; IMF, 2023). 
*   **Wholesale Funding Substitution:** To replace lost retail deposits and maintain asset portfolios (e.g., mortgages, corporate credit), commercial banks must turn to wholesale funding markets (such as commercial paper, repurchase agreements, and long-term senior unsecured debt) or central bank liquidity facilities. Because wholesale funding commands higher market risk premiums, average bank funding costs are projected to rise by 20 to 50 basis points for every 10% shift in retail deposits to rCBDC (Bindseil, 2020; Bank for International Settlements [BIS], 2021).

### B. Degradation of Basel III Regulatory Liquidity Metrics
The structural shift from retail deposits to wholesale funding negatively affects regulatory compliance under the Basel III framework, specifically regarding the **Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)** and the **Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR)**.

$$\text{LCR} = \frac{\text{High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA)}}{\text{Total Net Cash Outflows over 30 Days}} \ge 100\%$$

$$\text{NSFR} = \frac{\text{Available Stable Funding (ASF)}}{\text{Required Stable Funding (RSF)}} \ge 100\%$$

```
   Liquidity Metric Shifts Under CBDC Migration:
   
   Asset Side                              Liability Side
   +-----------------------+              +-----------------------+
   | HQLA (Reserves)  [-10]|              | Retail Deposits  [-10]|  (LCR run-off: 5%)
   | Loans / Other    [  0]|              | Wholesale Debt   [ +5]|  (LCR run-off: 25-100%)
   +-----------------------+              +-----------------------+
   
   Resulting Impact:
   * Net Cash Outflows (Denominator) INCREASE due to higher run-off rates of wholesale debt.
   * HQLA (Numerator) DECREASES due to reserve drain to Central Bank.
   * LCR drops, forcing banks to shrink illiquid loan books or purchase expensive HQLA bonds.
```

1.  **LCR Transmission:** Under Basel III standards, stable retail deposits carry a conservative run-off assumption of 5%, whereas non-operational wholesale funding carries run-off assumptions ranging from 25% to 100%. When $100 of retail deposits exit to an rCBDC and are partially replaced by $50 of short-term wholesale debt, the required HQLA denominator increases while actual HQLA reserves decline by the net outflow, depressing the bank's LCR (Bank for International Settlements, 2021).
2.  **NSFR Transmission:** Retail deposits receive an Available Stable Funding (ASF) factor of 90%–95%, whereas short-term wholesale market funding receives an ASF factor of 0%–50%. Replacing retail deposits with short-term wholesale liabilities reduces total ASF, forcing banks to shrink their long-term illiquid asset portfolios (such as commercial real estate and business loans) or issue expensive long-term debt.

### C. Run-Velocity Dynamics and Systemic Stress Mechanics
In traditional banking crises, bank runs are constrained by physical cash distribution limits (e.g., branch queues, ATM withdrawal caps) or wire transfer processing delays across business days. 

*   **Frictionless Flight-to-Safety:** An rCBDC introduces a digital, credit-risk-free balance sheet held directly at the central bank. In periods of localized bank distress, digital bank runs can occur at algorithmic speed (24/7/365 settlement without counterparty risk), accelerating the rate at which medium-sized or regional institutions lose liquidity (Ahnert et al., 2022).
*   **Contagion Risk:** The immediate availability of an rCBDC lowers conversion friction, raising the probability of self-fulfilling liquidity panics unless central bank lending facilities are modified to respond automatically.

### D. Architectural Countermeasures and Parameter Design
G7 central banks intend to implement design safeguards to limit structural disintermediation and run risk (European Central Bank, 2023; Bank of England, 2024):

```
       CBDC Remuneration & Holding Limit Architecture (Bindseil Model)
       
  Effective Yield (r)
          ^
          |
   r_CBDC |------------------+
          |                  |
          |                  |  Tier 2 Penal Rate (e.g., -200 bps or Tier 1 Cap)
        0 |------------------+---------------------------------------->
          |                  |                                 CBDC Holdings
          0             Holding Cap (T1) 
                       (e.g., €3,000 / £5,000)
```

1.  **Quantitative Holding Limits (Tier 1 Caps):** Imposing individual holding caps—such as €3,000 proposed by the ECB or £5,000–£20,000 evaluated by the Bank of England—restricts total aggregate outflow from the commercial banking sector. A €3,000 limit across the Eurozone population bounds potential aggregate deposit outflow to roughly €1 trillion (~7-8% of total Eurozone household deposits), preventing systemic disintermediation (European Central Bank, 2023).
2.  **Tiered Remuneration Systems:** As modeled by Bindseil (2020), Tier 1 holdings (up to $T_1$) yield zero or market-aligned interest, while Tier 2 holdings (exceeding $T_1$) yield zero or deeply negative rates ($r_{\text{Tier 2}} \ll 0$). This price-based disincentive deters large institutional or corporate balance sheet shifts into rCBDCs.
3.  **Reverse Waterfall Sweeping:** Integration with commercial bank accounts ensures that payments received in excess of individual holding caps automatically sweep into a designated commercial bank deposit account in real time, preventing inadvertent structural drain (European Central Bank, 2023).

## 2. Impacts on Monetary Policy Transmission Mechanics

### A. Deposit Betas and Interest Rate Pass-Through
Monetary policy pass-through to commercial bank deposit rates (the deposit beta, defined as $\beta = \Delta i_{\text{deposit}} / \Delta i_{\text{policy}}$) is historically incomplete due to commercial bank monopsony power over retail depositors.

$$\beta_{\text{deposit}} = \frac{\Delta i_{\text{deposit}}}{\Delta i_{\text{policy}}} < 1$$

*   **Competitive Pressure on Deposit Pricing:** The presence of a non-zero yield or low-friction alternative like an rCBDC raises the elasticity of retail deposits. To prevent deposit outflows, commercial banks must increase deposit rates faster and more completely in response to central bank rate hikes, raising the overall deposit beta closer to 1.0 (IMF, 2023).
*   **Symmetrical Credit Pass-Through:** A higher deposit beta accelerates the transmission of policy rate hikes to broad credit markets, sharpening the central bank's ability to cool inflation. Conversely, it compresses commercial bank Net Interest Margins (NIMs), reducing bank earnings retained for capital buffers.

```
       Monetary Pass-Through Channel Comparison
       
   Standard Banking Model:
   Policy Rate Shift (Δi) ===> Slow Deposit Rate Adjustment (Low β) ===> Delayed Credit Market Effect
   
   rCBDC-Augmented Model:
   Policy Rate Shift (Δi) ===> High Deposit Rate Adjustment (High β) ===> Immediate Credit Market Effect
                                (Driven by rCBDC Disintermediation Threat)
```

### B. Hardening of the Effective Lower Bound (ELB)
In deep recessions, central banks face constraints when lowering policy rates below zero due to the existence of physical cash ($i_{\text{cash}} = 0\%$).

*   **Non-Remunerated rCBDC ($i_{\text{CBDC}} = 0\%$):** Hardens the ELB at exactly 0%, as digital holdings eliminate the storage, transport, and insurance costs of physical currency. If central banks push commercial deposit rates below 0%, capital shifts into rCBDC without friction, rendering negative interest rate policies (NIRP) ineffective.
*   **Remunerated rCBDC ($i_{\text{CBDC}} \ne 0\%$):** If central banks establish technological and legal mechanics to apply negative interest rates to rCBDC balance sheet entries ($i_{\text{CBDC}} < 0\%$), the ELB is lowered further, expanding the theoretical scope for aggressive NIRP (Bindseil, 2020; BIS, 2021). However, G7 policy stances through 2026 strongly disfavor negative remuneration on public rCBDCs due to political resistance and legal challenges regarding privacy and property rights.

### C. Structural Alterations to the Bank Lending Channel
The classic bank lending channel posits that monetary tightening reduces central bank reserves, forcing banks to contract loan supply.

1.  **Amplified Transmission under Reserve Scarcity:** If rCBDC outflows drain commercial bank reserves, banks become more dependent on central bank credit facilities (e.g., ECB Main Refinancing Operations [MRO] or Fed Discount Window). This shifts the marginal cost of bank lending directly to central bank policy facility rates, enhancing central bank control over credit creation (IMF, 2023).
2.  **Central Bank Recycling Mechanisms:** To prevent credit crunches caused by rCBDC deposit flight, central banks can re-inject absorbed liquidity back into commercial banks via repo operations or long-term credit facilities (e.g., targeted long-term refinancing operations). While this neutralizes aggregate credit contraction, it turns the central bank into a structural financial intermediary, shifting credit risk allocation partly onto the monetary authority's balance sheet (BIS, 2021).

### D. Operational Frameworks and Corridor/Floor Dynamics
Post-2008 G7 central banking relies primarily on "floor systems" where central banks supply abundant excess reserves and pay Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB / DFR) to set short-term money market rates.

```
                  Floor System Operational Framework with rCBDC
                  
  Interest Rate
        |
   i_discount  |----------------------- (Ceiling: Lending Facility)
        |
        |          Demand Curve for Reserves
        |                   \
   i_IORB     |---------------------\------------------- (Policy Rate Floor)
        |                            \
        |                             \  <-- Reserve Drain via rCBDC shifts 
        |                              \     reserve volume LEFTWARD toward 
        |                               \    steep section of demand curve
        +------------------------------------------------------------->
                                        Reserves Quantity
```

*   **Reserves Drain and Rate Volatility:** If rCBDC adoption absorbs hundreds of billions in central bank liabilities, commercial bank reserve balances shrink. If reserves drop near the steep structural portion of the reserve demand curve, short-term money market rates (e.g., SOFR, ESTER, SONIA) become sensitive to daily liquidity shocks (Ahnert et al., 2022).
*   **Balance Sheet Expansion Requirement:** To preserve a stable floor system between 2027 and 2030, G7 central banks may need to permanently expand their asset portfolios (purchasing government securities or maintaining continuous repo facilities) to offset the structural reserve absorption of rCBDCs.

## 3. G7 Jurisdictional Trajectories & Comparative Projections (2027–2030)

### European Central Bank (Eurozone: France, Germany, Italy)
*   **Projected Status (2027–2030):** High likelihood of initial pilot deployment around 2027–2028, following the completion of the preparation phase and expected EU legislative approval (European Central Bank, 2023).
*   **Design Framework:** Two-tier model; strict individual holding limit (~€3,000); non-remunerated ($i_{\text{CBDC}} = 0\%$); reverse waterfall linking to commercial bank accounts.
*   **Liquidity & Transmission Impact:** Disintermediation risks are bounded by the €3,000 cap. Aggregate bank deposit loss is capped at ~€800B to €1T across the Eurozone. Monetary policy pass-through is expected to see slight acceleration in retail deposit rates, while the ECB maintains balance sheet recycling via regular MRO/LTRO injections.

### Bank of England (United Kingdom)
*   **Projected Status (2027–2030):** Possible production roll-out between 2028 and 2030, contingent on formal authorization by HM Treasury following technical design phases (Bank of England, 2024).
*   **Design Framework:** Proposed holding cap of £5,000 to £20,000 per adult; non-remunerated; private-sector wallet provision via API access to central bank ledger.
*   **Liquidity & Transmission Impact:** Modeling by the BoE suggests a potential 10% to 20% reduction in commercial bank retail deposits under a £20,000 cap, which could increase UK bank funding costs by 15–35 bps and slightly contract private sector credit unless offset by BoE repo facilities (Bank of England, 2024).

### Bank of Japan (Japan)
*   **Projected Status (2027–2030):** Technical pilot ongoing; institutional decisions anticipated around 2026/2027. Full-scale launch between 2028 and 2030 remains conditional on social consensus and private payment ecosystem co-existence (Bank of Japan, 2023).
*   **Design Framework:** Strong focus on resilience against natural disasters (offline capability); potential tiered holding caps; zero interest rate alignment.
*   **Liquidity & Transmission Impact:** Japanese regional banks depend heavily on retail deposits. Consequently, the BoJ is expected to implement conservative holding limits (e.g., < ¥1 million) to prevent disintermediation in secondary and tertiary regional markets (Bank of Japan, 2023).

### Federal Reserve System (United States)
*   **Projected Status (2027–2030):** Low probability of retail CBDC (rCBDC) implementation due to political opposition and legislative requirements for explicit Congressional authorization. Wholesale CBDC (wCBDC) and tokenized reserve pilot initiatives are more likely to progress (Ahnert et al., 2022).
*   **Design Framework:** Focus on institutional interbank settlement, cross-border payments, and tokenized commercial bank deposits rather than direct retail accounts.
*   **Liquidity & Transmission Impact:** Retail liquidity structure remains largely unchanged by central bank liabilities. Policy transmission continues through established floor mechanisms (IORB and ON RRP rates).

### Bank of Canada (Canada)
*   **Projected Status (2027–2030):** Contingency stance; public development slowed in late 2023 in favor of payment system modernization, maintaining readiness to deploy if private stablecoins or foreign CBDCs gain adoption (Bank of Canada, 2023).
*   **Design Framework:** Technical specifications prepared for rapid deployment if triggered; focus on universal accessibility and zero remuneration.
*   **Liquidity & Transmission Impact:** Minimal baseline impact expected during 2027–2030 unless private stablecoin adoption accelerates, triggering the deployment of Canada's contingency framework.

## Assessment

For 2027–2030, the defensible projection is **not a single G7-wide effect**, but a set of outcomes determined by four design variables:

1. **Wholesale or retail issuance**
2. **Remuneration and its responsiveness to the policy rate**
3. **Holding limits and access**
4. **Whether commercial banks or only the central bank operate customer wallets**

These choices determine whether CBDC changes banks’ liabilities, merely reclassifies funds, or changes how policy rates reach households and firms. The central-bank research literature emphasizes that CBDC adoption will vary substantially by design and country rather than follow one common template (Bank of Canada, n.d.; Bank of France, n.d.; BIS, n.d.).

### A new mechanism: distinguish three balance-sheet effects

The key analytical distinction missing from a simple “deposits leave banks” narrative is that CBDC can have three different effects:

| Implementation | Effect on commercial-bank deposits | Effect on bank liquidity | Monetary-policy consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Direct wallet; non-remunerated; capped** | Modest substitution from deposits into CBDC | Central-bank reserves drain when wallets are funded; banks replace reserves through normal monetary operations, but retain most funding relationships | Slightly stronger cash-like constraint on deposit rates; little direct gain in policy pass-through |
| **Direct wallet; remunerated or uncapped** | Potentially substantial and stress-sensitive deposit migration | Larger and more volatile reserve outflows; greater reliance on wholesale funding | Stronger effective floor under deposit rates and potentially faster policy transmission, but greater liquidity risk |
| **Bank-held retail wallet** | Little or no initial change in consolidated bank deposits | Primarily changes the composition and velocity of bank liabilities | Improves payment efficiency but may add little to monetary-policy transmission beyond existing direct-debit and online-banking channels |

The first row reveals an important qualification: **CBDC does not necessarily reduce total bank funding when commercial banks issue wallet balances**. It can instead create a *currency-competition margin* without wholesale disintermediation. The final row similarly explains why rapid adoption of “CBDC” need not imply a major monetary-policy discontinuity.

## Projection by transmission channel

### 1. Commercial-bank liquidity

#### Baseline expectation: manageable but more volatile liquidity

The most plausible 2027–2030 baseline is **greater day-to-day variation in reserve demand without, by itself, a systemic contraction in aggregate bank credit**.

The causal chain is:

1. A customer transfers funds from a commercial-bank account to a direct CBDC wallet.
2. The transfer reduces the customer’s bank deposit and normally the bank’s settlement balances at the central bank.
3. The central bank supplies reserves through its operating framework as banks manage settlement needs.
4. Banks therefore experience a change in the **composition and timing of their liabilities**, not necessarily an equal permanent loss of funding.
5. If adoption is capped and non-remunerated, the flow remains small relative to banks’ wider funding bases.
6. If remuneration is attractive or holdings are uncapped, migration can become self-reinforcing: better remuneration causes outflows, and outflows induce banks to compete more aggressively for deposits, raising their funding costs and potentially their loan rates.

Thus, projected effects on banks are likely to be heterogeneous:

- **Deposit stability:** somewhat lower during episodes of market stress, especially if CBDC is perceived as a flight-to-safety asset.
- **Funding costs:** higher for banks exposed to household deposits and limited access to sticky institutional funding.
- **Liquidity forecasting:** more difficult because wallet demand can react rapidly to remuneration changes, policy-rate expectations, or stress.
- **Credit allocation:** potentially more conservative at banks that lose deposits, although the effect on aggregate lending is uncertain because banks can replace deposits with wholesale funding when solvent and sufficiently liquid.

This direction is consistent with the official analyses reviewed by the Bank of Canada and the Bank of France: deposit substitution and bank disintermediation are central risks, but their severity depends principally on design parameters (Bank of Canada, n.d.; Bank of France, n.d.).

#### Stress scenario

The largest downside is not ordinary adoption but a rapid conversion of deposits into CBDC during a funding shock. A risk-free central-bank liability can then be more attractive than a bank deposit, while banks cannot simultaneously replace every lost deposit. The resulting mechanism is:

> deposit outflow → reserve and wholesale-funding pressure → higher marginal funding cost → tighter credit standards or asset sales → further depositor anxiety.

CBDC would amplify this mechanism only if it is directly accessible, remunerated sufficiently to compete with deposits, or not tightly capped. Holding limits, exchange controls, wallet-access restrictions, and temporary limits on transfer volumes would weaken it, although such restrictions would also reduce the CBDC’s usefulness as a general-purpose payment instrument.

### 2. Monetary-policy transmission

The projected effect differs according to what the CBDC is intended to do.

#### Case A: Non-remunerated retail CBDC

If the CBDC pays no interest, it is mainly a payments instrument. It does **not** provide an interest-bearing floor under commercial-bank deposit rates. Rather, it creates a cash-like alternative that limits how far banks can reduce deposit rates in a low-rate environment.

Under this design:

- Policy-rate changes still travel through existing deposit, lending, and asset-price channels.
- Faster settlement can reduce payment frictions and may slightly improve the speed of cash-transfer transmission.
- There is no major new portfolio-balancing channel, because holding CBDC does not compensate savers for bearing duration or default risk.
- During easing, funds may move from CBDC back to deposits when deposit rates become more attractive; during tightening, the reverse may occur.

The resulting projected effect is therefore a **small improvement in payment efficiency but little structural change in monetary-policy effectiveness**.

#### Case B: Remunerated retail CBDC linked to the policy rate

If the central bank pays an interest rate tied to the policy rate, the CBDC changes the portfolio choices available to the public. If its remuneration exceeds the return on comparable deposits, households and firms have an incentive to hold CBDC instead. This produces two effects:

1. **Portfolio-balancing effect:** funds move into CBDC when its remuneration is attractive relative to deposits.
2. **Rate-floor effect:** commercial banks need not offer deposit rates materially below the CBDC rate if customers can readily convert deposits into CBDC.

The second channel can strengthen transmission from the central bank’s policy rate to household and corporate deposit rates. It can also make monetary policy more effective near the effective lower bound, because the central bank can provide a remunerated reserve-like instrument to the non-bank public.

The cost is greater exposure to bank deposit disintermediation and potentially more volatile bank funding. Consequently, an interest-bearing CBDC could produce **faster monetary-policy transmission but less stable bank funding**—a genuine trade-off rather than an unqualified improvement.

#### Case C: Wholesale CBDC

A wholesale CBDC primarily changes settlement and dealer balance-sheet incentives. It may:

- Reduce settlement failures and gross settlement needs;
- Change banks’ incentives to hold reserves or make intraday credit to counterparties;
- Alter the distribution of liquidity shocks across dealers;
- Affect the transmission of monetary policy through money markets rather than household deposit substitution.

For G7 economies, wholesale issuance could therefore influence the **financial-market transmission channel** before retail CBDCs materially alter the bank-deposit channel. Its effects should not be inferred from retail-CBDC adoption figures.

### 3. The central-bank liquidity distinction

A further implication is that CBDC adoption can shift the location of liquidity without eliminating it:

> More CBDC balances outside banks can mean more central-bank liabilities to the public and fewer commercial-bank deposits, while the central bank simultaneously supplies or drains reserves as necessary to meet settlement demand.

Therefore:

- **Commercial-bank liquidity** can deteriorate because deposits or other stable funding become less available.
- **Central-bank liquidity provision** can remain ample if the operating framework accommodates CBDC settlement.
- **Systemwide payment liquidity** may improve if settlement is faster and more reliable.

A simple contraction in bank deposits is thus not evidence of a systemwide monetary shortage. The relevant test is whether banks can meet settlement obligations with available reserves and stable funding under stress.

## G7 outlook for 2027–2030

The central policy projection for the period is a **phased, segmented rollout rather than simultaneous universal retail adoption**. Official work in Canada, France, the United Kingdom, and international BIS analysis points toward continued experimentation and design refinement rather than one common deployment template (Bank of Canada, n.d.; Bank of France, n.d.; Bank of England/UK public-sector material cited in the thread, n.d.; BIS, n.d.).

The likely sequence is:

1. **2027–2028:** pilots, legal preparation, privacy and AML controls, and integration with existing payment rails. Direct effects on aggregate liquidity should remain limited.
2. **2028–2029:** possible expansion where legal and operational readiness permits, initially with stronger safeguards against deposit migration.
3. **By 2030:** a larger installed base may improve settlement efficiency, but macro effects will remain heterogeneous because the countries are likely to differ in remuneration, wallet architecture, holding limits, and the role assigned to banks.

The forecast should therefore be expressed conditionally:

- **If implementation remains limited and bank-integrated:** immaterial effects on aggregate bank liquidity; modest gains in payment speed; little change in monetary-policy transmission.
- **If adoption becomes substantial but capped and non-remunerated:** moderately more volatile deposit and reserve flows; stronger cash-like discipline on deposit pricing; limited systemic risk.
- **If adoption becomes substantial, uncapped, and remunerated:** significant deposit migration and funding-cost effects; potentially stronger policy-rate pass-through and a firmer effective floor under deposit rates; elevated stress-period liquidity risk.

## Bottom line

The principal projection for 2027–2030 is a shift from an **unresolved question about whether CBDC exists** to an unresolved question about **who owns the customer interface, who bears the funding effect, and how remuneration behaves**. Most plausible implementations should improve payment and settlement efficiency while leaving aggregate commercial-bank liquidity and the overall monetary-policy transmission mechanism only moderately changed. Large effects are possible, but they would arise from a specific combination of high adoption, substitutability with deposits, and inadequate safeguards—not from CBDC issuance alone.

## Bottom line

No defensible public forecast gives a single G7-wide figure for CBDC-driven deposit losses, bank liquidity needs, or changes in policy-rate transmission during 2027-2030. Outcomes depend on whether a jurisdiction issues a retail CBDC, its holding and remuneration rules, distribution model, and central-bank liquidity response. Treat this period as scenario analysis, not a quantified forecast.

If households move deposits into a retail CBDC, banks lose deposit funding and the reserve assets used to settle those transfers. That can raise marginal funding costs and increase liquidity-management pressure, especially during stress. It does not mechanically imply an equal loss of lending: central-bank refinancing, asset sales, replacement funding, and changes in lending terms can alter the result. Holding limits, low or zero remuneration, and automatic transfers of excess balances back to bank accounts can constrain routine substitution, but may not remove incentives to move funds quickly during a confidence shock.

For monetary policy, a CBDC could make bank deposit rates more responsive to policy rates by giving customers a closer substitute for bank deposits. That same substitution could weaken or change the bank-lending channel by making bank funding less stable or more expensive. A non-interest-bearing CBDC would not itself provide a direct policy-rate instrument. A remunerated CBDC could transmit policy rates directly to holders, but would also intensify competition with bank deposits. Neither effect has a reliable G7-wide magnitude for 2027-2030.

## Liquidity: mechanisms and conditions

**Deposit substitution.** Retail CBDC is a central-bank liability. When a customer exchanges a bank deposit for CBDC, the customer’s bank deposit liability falls; settlement also reduces that bank’s reserve balance, unless offset by incoming payments or central-bank operations. Banks may replace lost funding with other deposits, market borrowing, asset sales, or central-bank credit. The consequences for lending therefore depend on substitution costs and banks’ responses, not on a one-for-one mechanical link between deposit outflows and lower credit.

**Routine use versus stress.** A CBDC designed mainly for payments, with low holding limits and no interest, may attract balances for transactions without becoming a major savings vehicle. In a crisis, however, its status as a direct central-bank claim and ease of transfer could make conversion from bank deposits faster. The size of that risk depends on access, conversion limits, operational design, and the credibility of deposit insurance and liquidity support. The possibility of faster outflows is not evidence that a large outflow will occur.

**Safeguards involve trade-offs.** Holding limits and automatic “waterfall” arrangements, where balances above a limit transfer to a linked bank account, can reduce persistent deposit substitution. They can also restrict use and complicate payment flows. A zero-interest design may reduce competition for deposits in ordinary conditions, but does not prevent flight to safety. Conversely, central-bank lending can replace lost bank liquidity, but may increase banks’ reliance on central-bank funding and collateral.

**Liquidity is not solvency.** A transfer from bank deposits into CBDC can create a funding and settlement need. It does not by itself make a bank insolvent. Insolvency depends on asset values and capital; liquidity stress concerns a bank’s ability to meet payments when due. Analysis that treats every CBDC holding as an equivalent, permanent contraction in bank lending confuses these channels.

## Monetary-policy transmission

**Deposit-rate competition.** When CBDC offers a safe alternative, customers may be more willing to move funds if bank deposit rates lag policy rates. Banks could then raise deposit rates sooner or accept deposit losses. This may sharpen policy-rate pass-through to deposit rates, while raising banks’ funding costs. The net effect on borrowers is not predetermined: banks may reprice loans, reduce margins, change lending volumes, or replace funding.

**Direct remuneration channel.** If a CBDC pays interest linked to the policy rate, a central bank could change the return paid on CBDC balances directly. This creates a potential direct channel to holders. It does not guarantee faster transmission to all household and business borrowing rates, which still depend on competition, credit risk, bank balance sheets, and market structure. A non-remunerated CBDC lacks this direct interest-rate channel.

**Bank-lending channel.** If deposit funding becomes more sensitive to policy rates or more prone to outflow, banks may adjust credit supply and lending terms differently. That can modify the traditional bank-lending channel. The effect is conditional: central-bank refinancing may offset liquidity pressure, while collateral requirements, pricing, and access rules determine whether that refinancing supports credit.

**Cash and the effective lower bound.** A non-interest-bearing CBDC would resemble cash as a zero-yield nominal asset, rather than remove the constraint created by cash. Whether a remunerated CBDC could alter lower-bound dynamics depends on its design and on continued access to cash. Claims that CBDC necessarily enables negative rates or “helicopter money” go beyond what follows from issuing digital central-bank money.

## What can be said about G7, 2027-2030

The question groups together seven economies, but their legal decisions, payment systems, and CBDC designs are not uniform. Official research and consultation documents establish possible designs and risks, not a common implementation schedule or numerical forecast. The ECB’s digital-euro work, the Bank of England and HM Treasury consultation, and the Federal Reserve’s public discussion document are jurisdiction-specific. They cannot support claims that all G7 members will launch retail CBDCs, or that any particular deposit-loss percentage will apply across the group.

Wholesale CBDC projects should also be kept separate from retail CBDCs. Wholesale arrangements concern settlement among financial institutions and may change settlement processes or liquidity management. They do not, by themselves, give households a new store of value that directly competes with bank deposits. Their effects on monetary transmission depend on market design and central-bank operations.

A useful 2027-2030 assessment should therefore report, by jurisdiction and design:

1. Retail or wholesale scope, access, and distribution model.
2. Holding limits, remuneration, and automatic balance-sweep rules.
3. Deposit and reserve flows under ordinary use and stress scenarios.
4. Bank replacement-funding costs, collateral needs, and lending responses.
5. Policy-rate pass-through to deposit rates, lending rates, and credit supply.
6. Central-bank liquidity operations that could offset reserve or funding shifts.

Public central-bank sources reviewed for this answer do not provide a standardized G7 census or a comparable forecast of these outcomes. Exact aggregate impacts remain unmeasured; numerical ranges would imply more evidence than the cited sources provide.

## What this Answer adds

The key distinction is between a CBDC’s possible effects and a quantified forecast. This answer separates retail deposit substitution from wholesale settlement, liquidity pressure from solvency, and direct policy-rate transmission from changes in bank lending. It also identifies the conditions that determine whether safeguards constrain ordinary substitution yet leave stress-period outflow risk. Those distinctions rule out a single G7-wide impact estimate on the available evidence.

**Short answer.** Between 2027 and 2030, CBDCs will have small, bounded effects on commercial-bank liquidity and almost no direct effect on monetary-policy transmission in the G7 — because, with one exception, no G7 economy will have a retail CBDC in general circulation during that window, and the one that might (the digital euro, first issuance possible in 2029) is designed specifically not to disintermediate banks: no interest, and a holding limit of about €3,000 per person. The real action in 2027–2030 is elsewhere — wholesale CBDC for interbank settlement, and private stablecoins forcing banks to compete on deposit rates. The liquidity risk that matters is not the steady state but a stress event: in a panic, a CBDC is the perfect run asset, and only the holding limits stand between that and a digital bank run.

## 1. Where the G7 actually stands

The global picture first. The Bank for International Settlements' 2024 survey of 93 central banks, published 22 August 2025, found 91% exploring a retail or wholesale CBDC, with wholesale work generally further advanced than retail, and more than one in three jurisdictions saying the rise of stablecoins had accelerated their work (cryptoinfrastructure.io, 2026). The Atlantic Council's tracker counted 146 jurisdictions exploring a CBDC in May 2026, 77 at an advanced stage, 41 running pilots — and only three with a launched retail CBDC: the Bahamas, Jamaica and Nigeria (osakawire, 2026). Exploration is near-universal; issuance to the public is rare.

Inside the G7 the split is three ways. The euro area (France, Germany, Italy) is the furthest along: the ECB completed its investigation phase in 2023, is in a preparation phase running through 2025–2026, moved to its next phase on 30 October 2025, expects EU legislation in 2026, a pilot with first transactions from mid-2027, and readiness for a possible first issuance in 2029, at a development cost of about €1.3 billion and running cost of about €320 million a year (douglasinsights, 2026; eco.com, 2026). The UK is a step behind and deliberately undecided: the Bank of England and HM Treasury completed their 2023 consultation on a digital pound and moved into a design phase, but as of 2026 the Bank has emphasised that no decision to issue has been made — the work preserves the option to launch — and on 4 March 2026 the Bank said it and the Treasury would decide later in 2026 whether to proceed or focus on other payment upgrades (eco.com, 2026; douglasinsights, 2026). The United States has gone the other way: the executive order of 23 January 2025 bars federal agencies from any action to establish, issue or promote a CBDC, the House passed the Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act 219–210 on 17 July 2025 (awaiting the Senate), and after the GENIUS stablecoin Act passed in 2025 the US is unlikely to pursue a retail CBDC in the near term — the Atlantic Council describes it as the only G20 country not exploring one, though the New York Fed still takes part in wholesale cross-border research through Project Agorá (eco.com, 2026; pareto-academy, 2026). I have no cited source in this session for Japan's or Canada's retail-CBDC decisions, so I do not assert their positions here; the mechanism analysis below applies to them through the same design variables (caps, remuneration, wholesale vs retail).

The live retail CBDCs are also a warning about adoption. In Nigeria, 98.5% of eNaira wallets sat unused in any given week a year after launch; Jamaica's JAM-DEX amounted to about 0.09% of currency in circulation in mid-2026; and an IMF review found the Bahamas' Sand Dollar accounted for less than 0.1% of currency in circulation (osakawire, 2026). Where a good private or public alternative already exists, retail CBDCs have struggled to find users — which is itself a forecast input: even a launched G7 retail CBDC would likely take years to reach volumes that move aggregate bank liquidity.

## 2. Commercial-bank liquidity: capped in normal times, a run channel in stress

The liquidity mechanism is mechanical. A retail CBDC is a direct liability of the central bank — the same credit risk as physical cash — so every unit held in a CBDC wallet is a unit not held as a commercial-bank deposit (eco.com, 2026). Uncapped, that is disintermediation: deposits fund bank lending, and a large shift would force banks to replace cheap deposit funding with wholesale funding or shrink their balance sheets. Every G7 design on the table prevents that by construction. The digital euro would pay no interest and would carry a holding limit — the ECB has tested hypothetical limits of up to €3,000 per person, and the Council of the EU's December 2025 position would have co-legislators set a maximum ceiling (for example €3,000 for individuals) within which the ECB sets and adjusts the actual limit, reviewed at least every two years (pareto-academy, 2026; whitehousecomms, 2026). The proposed digital-pound holding limit is £10,000–£20,000 (whitehousecomms, 2026). A per-person cap bounds the maximum deposit outflow arithmetically, and the design intent is explicit: "strict limits per wallet to avoid disintermediating commercial banks" (eco.com, 2026). My judgement: in normal times through 2030, the liquidity effect in the euro area and the UK is therefore small — measured in low single-digit percentages of household deposits at most, and only after launch, which for the euro area means 2029 at the earliest.

The stress case is the one the caps exist for. In a bank panic, a CBDC is the ideal flight asset: risk-free, digital, instant, and — unlike cash — without physical withdrawal limits. The cap is then doing real work: a €3,000 ceiling means a household can move at most €3,000 out of the banking system per person, which slows a run but does not stop one if the panic is about a specific bank rather than the system. That is the honest statement of the residual risk, and it is why the limit is a ceiling the ECB can adjust rather than a fixed number. Wholesale CBDC is a different liquidity story: it settles between banks and does not touch retail deposits at all, so its 2027–2030 effect is on settlement liquidity and cross-border payment speed (Project Agorá, mBridge), not on commercial-bank funding.

## 3. Monetary-policy transmission: remuneration is the switch, and the G7 designs leave it off

Transmission depends almost entirely on one design choice: does the CBDC pay interest? A remunerated CBDC at the policy rate would be a direct transmission channel — the central bank's rate would reach households' wallets without passing through banks' deposit pricing — and would put a floor under deposit rates, since no one would hold a zero-interest bank deposit when a risk-free CBDC pays the policy rate. But the digital euro would pay no interest (pareto-academy, 2026), and the same cash-like, non-remunerated design is the default for the G7 retail proposals in my sources. A non-remunerated, capped CBDC is economically close to digital cash: it changes the payment system, not the interest-rate channel. My judgement: through 2030, the direct transmission effect of G7 CBDCs is therefore approximately zero. The indirect effect is larger and runs through competition: US dollar-backed stablecoins, actively encouraged by the US administration from 2025, already shift payments and deposits outside the banking system, and that competitive pressure — not CBDC — is what will force G7 banks to pay more for deposits and transmit policy rates faster (whitehousecomms, 2026). Note the contrast outside the G7: Caixin reported in December 2025 that China's banks would pay interest on e-CNY wallet balances from January 2026 (cryptoinfrastructure.io, 2026) — a remunerated design, and the only one in my sources, which is exactly the design that would change transmission.

## 4. Forecast 2027–2030 (labelled as judgement)

Most likely path (roughly 65–75%): no G7 retail CBDC in general circulation before 2029; the digital euro pilots in 2027 and issues in 2029 at the earliest; the UK decides in late 2026 and, if it proceeds, launches years later; the US stays out. Bank liquidity effects stay bounded by caps and by slow adoption (the live-CBDC precedents above suggest take-up is the binding constraint, not the cap). Transmission effects stay near zero for the non-remunerated designs. The two things that would falsify this: a euro-area decision to remunerate the digital euro, which would convert it overnight from a payment instrument into a transmission channel; or a financial-stress event in which the CBDC's run-asset property is tested and the €3,000 ceiling is raised or suspended. Either would be visible in advance — in ECB publications for the first, in deposit-flow data for the second — so the forecast is checkable, not just asserted.

**What this Answer adds.** This is the first Answer on the Question. Its contribution is the dated G7 status map (digital euro pilot 2027 / issuance 2029, UK undecided, US banned — each with its source and date) joined to the mechanism that actually decides the Question's two outcomes: holding limits bound the liquidity effect, and non-remuneration switches the transmission effect off — plus the live-CBDC adoption evidence (eNaira, JAM-DEX, Sand Dollar) that bounds how fast any launched G7 CBDC could move aggregate deposits.
